_comment: Accumulated validation learnings consumed by AI mapping + repair prompts at generation time to avoid known pitfalls. Keyed by 'sourcetype::destFormat' and by 'destFormat' (format-wide). Appended automatically by the schema validator's repair flow. Safe to hand-edit.

cef: Assemble _raw as a single CEF:0 header + space-separated key=value extension; never emit one giant template-literal expression.
Reserved word 'in' must be accessed as __e['in'] inside eval expressions.

CEF extension expressions must READ real extracted source fields (src_ip, dest_ip, src_port) — the destField uses the CEF short name (src, dst, spt) but the expression value must reference the source field. Writing expression=src (the CEF name) when the parser produced src_ip yields empty output. This is the #1 CEF defect.
CEF 'rt' (receipt time) should be epoch milliseconds, not a human-readable date string. Convert the parsed timestamp before emitting rt.
Escape CEF extension values: backslash, equals, and newline in values must be escaped per the CEF spec to avoid breaking the key=value parsing.
CEF _raw MUST begin with 'CEF:0|' — never prepend a bare 'host' word or hostname. Put the hostname in the dvchost/dvc extension instead.

The Name (Activity) field must be human-readable and DIFFERENT from DeviceEventClassID. Never emit 'code|code' (e.g. '302016|302016'). If the source has only a numeric code, look up or synthesize a short label.

CEF LogSeverity is 0-10 where HIGHER = more severe. Syslog/ASA severity LEVEL is 0-7 where LOWER = more severe — you MUST invert it (e.g. CEF_sev ≈ 10 - level*1.3), not copy it. Reference the actual parsed field name (severity), not an invented one like cisco_severity.
Do NOT map the entire original log line into msg=. msg should be a SHORT human summary (<200 chars) or be omitted; the raw line is already represented by the structured extension fields.

Reference the EXACT field names the parser produced (severity, src_ip, dest_ip, transport). Do not invent variants like cisco_severity, srcaddr, or proto_name that no parse stage emits — they evaluate to null and the CEF field is dropped.
Always map the transport/protocol to CEF 'proto' and the parsed timestamp to _time (via a Cribl Auto Timestamp or eval) so events don't all share the pipeline processing time.

Parser output field names MUST match the canonical model the CEF spec reads: src_ip/dest_ip/src_port/dest_port/transport (NOT dst_ip/dst_port/proto). A dst_* vs dest_* mismatch silently drops the destination fields from the CEF extension. Normalize to dest_* in the parse stage.
CEF 'proto' should be a transport NAME (tcp/udp/icmp), not a raw IP protocol number. Convert numeric proto (6->tcp, 17->udp, 1->icmp, 58->ipv6-icmp) in the parser via a ternary or lookup.
CEF 'app' is the application/SERVICE name (HTTPS, DNS, SMTP) — never the protocol number. Do not let app fall back to proto.

Timestamp handling must accept an ALREADY-numeric epoch value: 13 digits = ms, 10 digits = seconds, otherwise parse as a date string. new Date(String(epochMs)) returns Invalid Date for a numeric-ms string, so _time/rt silently break and default to pipeline (wrong) time.
ocsf: Always set class_uid, category_uid, activity_id and type_uid as numbers, not strings.

checkpoint_firewall::nextgen: For OCSF/nextgen targets, class_uid, category_uid, type_uid, activity_id, and severity_id must ALL be numeric integers — never strings or label names; map Check Point action/product combinations to the correct OCSF numeric triplet before output.

Always parse the syslog header timestamp (MMM DD HH:MM:SS) into _time using a timestamp extraction function; never allow _time to default to pipeline processing time, which causes all events to share an identical wrong timestamp.

Do not repurpose process_name or command_line for security-domain fields like attack names or policy reasons; use dedicated fields such as attack_name, threat_name, or a reason field, and omit or null process/command fields when the source is network firewall traffic with no process context.
Resolve port numbers to application/service names when populating the application field, or at minimum use the service name from the Check Point 'service' field rather than a raw port number string.
Empty-string placeholders ('') for optional fields that are not present in the source event should be omitted entirely or set to null to avoid polluting the schema with meaningless values.

When mapping to OCSF/nextgen, differentiate class_uid and type_uid per event_type: firewall=4001/400101, IPS detection=different class, malware=detection finding class — never use a single value for all event types.

The 'orig' field in Check Point logs is the reporting device (firewall), not the traffic source; src_host should be resolved separately or left as the IP, and orig should map to a device/observer field.
When parsing syslog without explicit year, default to current year (not future year); validate epoch timestamps against expected date ranges before shipping.
VPN, user, and blade-specific contextual fields must be explicitly mapped to structured schema objects (vpn.peer, user.name, etc.) rather than dropped or left flat.
Preserve _raw in all nextgen pipeline outputs for auditability and fallback search; dropping it loses forensic fidelity.
Always nest OCSF observer, actor, src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, and metadata fields as objects rather than flattening them with underscore notation — OCSF is a strictly hierarchical schema.
Do not use severity_id=0 (Unknown) for Drop/Reject firewall actions; assign a meaningful severity based on policy context (e.g., severity_id=2 Low for routine drops).
Validate type_uid values against the specific OCSF class definition — type_uid must be a recognized enumeration value for the given class_uid, not an arbitrary computed integer.
Use status_id (numeric OCSF enum) instead of a free-text 'outcome' field; OCSF does not define a top-level 'outcome' string field in Network Activity or IPS Detection classes.
Avoid duplicating product information in both 'product' and 'app' fields; map product to metadata.product.name and remove the redundant flat 'app' field.
Ensure _time is in milliseconds (epoch ms) for OCSF compliance, and prefer the standard OCSF 'time' field name over '_time'.
checkpoint_firewall::ocsf: Always include the required OCSF 'metadata' wrapper object with at minimum metadata.version, metadata.product.name, and metadata.product.vendor_name before emitting any event.
Map Check Point src/dst/port fields into OCSF structured endpoint objects (src_endpoint:{ip,port}, dst_endpoint:{ip,port}) with integer port values, not flat string fields.

Derive class_uid dynamically from the Check Point 'product' or 'blade' field: SmartDefense/IPS -> 4002 (Intrusion Detection), Anti-Malware -> 4004 (Malware Activity), VPN-1/FireWall-1 -> 4001 (Network Activity); then compute type_uid = class_uid * 100 + activity_id.

Use only valid OCSF activity_id values for the target class — for Network Activity (4001): 1=Open, 2=Close, 3=Reset, 4=Fail, 99=Other. Map Accept->1, Drop/Reject->4. Never use invented names like 'Refuse'.
Parse source log timestamps into the OCSF 'time' integer field (epoch milliseconds); never leave all events with the same pipeline-ingestion timestamp as '_time'.
Always populate both the _id and string pair for severity, status, activity etc. — if severity_id is set, severity string must also be set consistently across all events.
For IPS/threat events, populate the OCSF 'attacks' array with structured technique objects; for malware events populate the 'malware' array — do not leave attack/malware_name as flat raw strings.

Always verify OCSF class_uid numeric values against the official schema registry — 4002 is Network Connection, not Intrusion Detection (which is 4003); mismatched class_uid invalidates type_uid and all downstream routing.
Infer traffic direction from IP address context (RFC1918 vs public): flows from public IPs to private destinations are Inbound; never default all events to Outbound.
Empty string ('') is worse than omitting optional OCSF sub-object fields like attacks[].technique.uid — either populate with real values or omit the field entirely to avoid failing schema validators.
The 'firewall_rule' object is not part of OCSF Network Activity (4001); rule metadata belongs in connection_info or unmapped to maintain schema conformance.
Always map the 'reason' or 'status_detail' field from block/drop events — it is critical context that should appear in OCSF status_detail or unmapped, never silently dropped.
OCSF metadata should always include logged_time, uid (generated), and profiles array even when the source does not provide them — these are required for interoperability.
Always include disposition_id in OCSF Network Activity events from firewall sources — it is the primary field conveying Allow(1)/Block(2)/Quarantine(3) and must not be replaced by status_id alone.

Verify class_uid values against the official OCSF schema registry (currently 1.9.0); in 1.9.0 class_uid=4003 is DNS Activity. IDS/IPS events should use class_uid=4001 (Network Activity) with security_control profile or class_uid=2001 (Security Finding) depending on context — do not force IDS/IPS onto 4003.
Do not place the firewall rule number in connection_info.boundary_id — boundary_id is a numeric enum; rule numbers belong in firewall_rule.uid and optionally replicated in unmapped.
For security product events (IPS, Anti-Malware, SmartDefense), populate finding_info and/or malware objects rather than leaving attack/malware details only in attacks[] or unmapped.
Never emit attacks[].tactic as an empty object {}; omit the tactic key entirely when no tactic data is available to avoid schema validation failures.
Severity should only be mapped from source data; when the source event has no severity field, use severity_id=0 (Unknown) rather than inventing a Low/Informational assignment.
NAT fields (xlatesrc, nat_rule) should map to OCSF network_proxy or nat_endpoint structures, not unmapped, as OCSF 1.9.0 provides defined objects for network address translation.

Always map the action/rule_action field from Check Point logs to OCSF disposition and use it to derive activity_id rather than hardcoding; for firewall traffic logs, action=Accept/Drop/Reject directly determines the network activity type.

Check Point pipe-delimited fields like rule_name, rule_uid, ifdir, ifname, loguid, origin, and layer_name are high-value and must be explicitly extracted and mapped — do not rely only on src/dst/user; use regex or key=value parsing on the full message body.
Never hardcode product.name to a specific Check Point product name ('SmartDefense') when the source explicitly carries product=Firewall; always read the product field from the source.
severity_id must be derived from a source field (e.g., severity, alert level) or set to 0 (Unknown) if no source field exists; hardcoding to 5 (Critical) for all events is misleading and incorrect.

Empty nested objects (dst_endpoint:{}, connection_info:{}, traffic:{}) should be omitted or populated — emitting empty containers wastes space and implies fields were evaluated but found empty rather than absent from the source.

Prefer a single canonical time representation in OCSF (epoch seconds integer or ISO-8601 string); do not emit both _time in seconds and time in milliseconds simultaneously without clear documentation of the intent.
Always map the firewall action field (action=Accept/Drop) to OCSF disposition_id — this is a required field for Network Activity and the value is always present in Check Point logs.
Do not hardcode metadata.product.name; read it from the source product= field and translate only when necessary (e.g., 'Firewall' → 'Check Point Firewall').

Check Point logs consistently carry rule_name, rule_uid, rule_action, ifdir, ifname, and origin — build explicit mappings for all of these to OCSF firewall_rule, connection_info.direction, and device.ip respectively.
Never emit empty OCSF sub-objects (actor.user: {}, connection_info: {}, traffic: {}) — either populate them or omit them entirely, as empty required objects fail OCSF schema validation.
severity_id must be derived from a source severity/priority indicator or defaulted to 0 (Unknown); fabricating it as Critical (5) on all events is worse than omitting it.
In Check Point logs, 'origin' is the gateway/sensor IP — map it to device.ip or observer, NOT dst_endpoint.ip; actual traffic src/dst IPs come from 'src' and 'dst' fields.

When computing metadata.logged_time (processing time), validate the resulting epoch is plausible (within a few years of the event time) — a bug producing year-2026 timestamps from 2023 events indicates a unit mismatch (ms vs s) or incorrect base value.

Check Point logs often carry both 'ifdir' (interface direction) and 'conn_direction' (connection direction) — both should be captured; when they differ, prefer conn_direction for connection_info.direction and note ifdir separately.
Avoid duplicating the same value in both a mapped OCSF field (metadata.uid) and the unmapped object (unmapped.loguid) — pick one canonical location.
Do not hardcode device.name from a field known to be masked/redacted (originsicname); prefer the actual hostname for device.name and omit or use a separate field for SIC names.
Always derive metadata.product.name from the source product= field rather than hardcoding a product family name; Check Point logs explicitly carry product=Firewall, product=VPN, etc.

For Check Point firewall logs, action/rule_action=Accept|Drop|Reject must be mapped to OCSF disposition_id (1=Allowed, 2=Blocked) and activity_id should reflect the actual network event type, not be hardcoded.
Never hardcode severity_id without a source field to derive it from; if no severity field exists in the source, use severity_id=0 (Unknown) or omit it.
All source key=value pairs that cannot be mapped to a canonical OCSF field should be preserved in an unmapped_data map object to avoid information loss.

Empty container objects (src_endpoint={}, dst_endpoint={}, connection_info={}, traffic={}) should be omitted from output when the source carries no values to populate them — empty objects are noise in OCSF and can break downstream schema validation.
ifdir and conn_direction fields must be parsed and translated to OCSF connection_info.direction_id (1=Inbound, 2=Outbound, 3=Lateral, 99=Other).
The firewall origin IP (origin= field in Check Point logs) is the reporting device IP and should be mapped to device.ip, not discarded.
Always derive metadata.product.name directly from the source 'product' field rather than hardcoding a vendor-specific sub-product name.

Check Point pipe-delimited fields (action, rule_action, rule_name, rule_uid, ifdir, ifname, conn_direction, origin, loguid) must each be explicitly parsed and mapped to their OCSF counterparts: disposition_id, firewall_rule.name, firewall_rule.uid, connection_info.direction, src_endpoint.interface_name, metadata.uid.
Never hardcode severity_id; derive it from source severity/priority fields or set to 0 (Unknown) when no source signal exists.
Empty OCSF objects (dst_endpoint:{}, connection_info:{}, traffic:{}) should be omitted or populated; leaving them as empty objects wastes space and signals incomplete parsing to downstream consumers.
The 'origin' field in Check Point logs is the firewall's own IP and should be mapped to device.ip or observer endpoint, not confused with src/dst endpoint — but it must not be silently dropped.
Parse all key=value pairs from the raw syslog message before any field mapping — if parsing fails, all downstream mappings produce empty objects.
Event timestamp must be extracted from the syslog header (e.g., 'Jun 25 00:03:17') and converted to epoch; never use pipeline processing time as the event time.

Dynamic fields like product name, action→activity_id, and severity must be mapped per-event from parsed source values, not hardcoded; use lookup tables for action→OCSF activity_id and severity string→severity_id.
OCSF class_uid should be selected based on the blade/product type (e.g., IPS → 4002 Detection Finding, Firewall → 4001 Network Activity) rather than a single hardcoded value for all events.

All populated source fields (src, dst, s_port, service, proto, user, orig, rule, reason, xlatesrc, malware_name, vpn_peer, enc_algo) must be explicitly mapped to their OCSF target paths; validate that no container objects are left empty after pipeline execution.
checkpoint_firewall::cef: CEF _raw must begin exactly with 'CEF:0|' — never prepend hostnames, 'host', or any other prefix; if a syslog header exists, strip it before constructing the CEF string.

Always use official CEF extension key names from the CEF specification (src, dst, dpt, spt, proto, act, dvchost, suser, msg, rt, etc.) — verbose descriptive names like 'SourceIP' or 'TransportProtocol' are not valid CEF keys.
When mapping multi-product sources like Check Point, derive the CEF DeviceProduct field dynamically from the source 'product' field rather than hardcoding a single product name for all events.
Preserve all source-specific fields (VPN_peer, VPN_tunnel, malware_name, blade) by mapping them to appropriate CEF custom string or flex fields (cs1-cs6, flexString1-2) to avoid data loss.
Map the syslog timestamp to the CEF 'rt' (receipt time) extension field to maintain temporal fidelity in the output.
Always convert syslog timestamps to epoch milliseconds for the CEF 'rt' field; human-readable date strings are non-conformant with the CEF specification.
Omit empty/null cs1–cs6 and cs1Label–cs6Label pairs from the CEF extension string entirely; including them as empty strings pollutes the extension and may cause parser errors.
Parse _time from the actual event timestamp (syslog header) rather than processing time; identical _time across all events indicates the timestamp extraction step was skipped.
In CEF extensions, csNLabel keys must immediately precede their corresponding csN value keys (e.g., cs1Label=Rule Number cs1=5), not follow them.
Use cn1/cn1Label for numeric values like rule numbers rather than cs1/cs1Label, which are reserved for string values per the CEF specification.
When source logs contain a 'reason' or descriptive field, prefer it for 'msg' over synthetic pipeline-constructed strings to preserve original log fidelity.
Always map transport-layer protocol (TCP/UDP) to the CEF 'proto' extension key, not 'app'; reserve 'app' for application-layer protocol identification (HTTP, DNS, FTP, etc.).

Omit optional CEF extension fields (cs1-cs6, suser, etc.) entirely from both _raw and JSON output when they have no value — empty key=value pairs in CEF extensions and empty string JSON fields both violate CEF best practices and pollute downstream schemas.
Strip internal pipeline working fields (prefixed __ or similar) before finalizing output events; these are processing artifacts and must not appear in delivered schema.
Validate that all output events are complete before finalizing — truncated _raw fields (event 8) indicate a pipeline buffer or string-length limit issue that must be caught in QA.

For Check Point CEF, the 'reason' field from the source log should be mapped to a dedicated CEF extension (e.g., 'reason' or a cs* field), not only surfaced in the free-text 'msg' field, to enable structured querying.
checkpoint_firewall::commonsecuritylog: CommonSecurityLog/CEF output MUST include a _raw field formatted as 'CEF:0|DeviceVendor|DeviceProduct|DeviceVersion|DeviceEventClassID|Activity|LogSeverity|extensions' — this is non-negotiable for the format.

All field names must use the exact CommonSecurityLog column names (DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, SourcePort, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, TimeGenerated, LogSeverity) — custom aliases like src_ip, dst_ip, action, timestamp break schema conformance.

Check Point-specific fields (attack, malware_name, reason, xlatesrc, VPN fields) should be mapped to CEF extension fields such as DeviceCustomString1-6, Reason, or AdditionalExtensions rather than dropped or placed in unrelated fields like process_name/command_line.
Internal pipeline metadata fields like 'sourcetype' and 'outcome' should be stripped before output unless they are defined in the target schema.
When severity is absent from source events (non-threat firewall accepts), LogSeverity should be assigned a default value (e.g., 'Low' or '3') rather than emitting an empty string.
Always parse the syslog header timestamp (e.g., 'Jun 25 00:03:17') into a per-event _time epoch; never allow all events to share the same pipeline processing timestamp.

CEF DeviceEventClassID must be a stable, product-defined event category identifier — never use a dynamic per-log value like a firewall rule number; use a mapped constant such as 'FW-ACCEPT', 'FW-DROP', 'IPS-DROP', or a numeric type code instead.

CEF _raw extension key labels (e.g., cs2Label=VPNPeer) must exactly match the corresponding parsed JSON field value (DeviceCustomString2Label='VPNPeer') — any normalization or spacing difference creates schema inconsistency.

For CommonSecurityLog target, always populate DeviceAddress (orig IP), DestinationHostName where available, and avoid duplicating already-mapped fields (like xlatesrc) in both a dedicated field and AdditionalExtensions.
When source severity field is absent, document the default severity-mapping heuristic (e.g., action→severity table) and apply it consistently rather than leaving it implicit.

Map SourceTranslatedAddress to the standard CEF extension key 'csta' (or 'sourceTranslatedAddress') in _raw, not to cs6/cs6Label=NATSrc, to maintain CEF compliance and correct CommonSecurityLog parsing.
Do not re-emit fields in AdditionalExtensions if they have already been mapped to a named CEF extension field (e.g., reason, suser); AdditionalExtensions should only carry truly unmapped fields.
Map the Check Point rule number to DeviceCustomNumber1/cn1Label='RuleNum' rather than only AdditionalExtensions, as rule number is a first-class audit field in firewall log schemas.
When the source syslog has no year, validate the year inference logic — defaulting to current wall-clock year can produce future-dated events if logs are replayed or timezone offsets are mishandled.
For IPS/Anti-Malware events with an explicit severity field in the source, carry that value through to LogSeverity exactly rather than deriving it from action alone.
checkpoint_firewall::cim: Always parse the syslog header timestamp into _time using strptime — never let all events share the pipeline execution time.
CIM Network Traffic datamodel uses 'tag=network tag=communicate' for classification — do not inject OCSF fields (class_uid, category_uid as strings) into a CIM pipeline.

For IPS/IDS events from Check Point SmartDefense or IPS blade, always populate 'ids_type' (e.g., 'network') and 'category' alongside 'signature' and 'severity' to satisfy the CIM Intrusion Detection datamodel.
Map 'application' to a resolved service name (dns, http, https, smb) using a lookup against the port number — never assign a raw port number string to the CIM 'application' field.
Remove or alias vendor-native fields (src, dst, proto, s_port) after mapping to CIM canonical names to avoid namespace pollution and duplicate fields in the output.
Always extract and normalize '_time' from the syslog header timestamp as epoch — its absence breaks nearly all CIM-based searches and correlations.
Map source IP to 'src' (not 'src_ip') and ensure destination uses 'dest' exclusively — these are the canonical CIM Network Traffic field names; use 'src_ip' only as an alias if needed.
Omit fields entirely when they have no value rather than setting them to empty string — empty string pollution breaks isnull() checks and tag-based datamodel acceleration in Splunk CIM.
For IDS/IPS events, set 'ids_type' based on the blade/product: endpoint/anti-malware products should use 'host', network IPS/SmartDefense should use 'network'.
CIM 'tag' fields should be multi-value (array) with individual values like 'network' and 'communicate' separately, not concatenated as a single string.
Avoid duplicate fields with different casing (VPN_peer vs vpn_peer) — normalize all field names to lowercase CIM conventions and drop the original case variant after mapping.

Always ensure 'src' (source IP) is extracted and mapped for every Check Point firewall event — it is the most critical CIM Network Traffic field and commonly dropped when pipelines focus only on destination mapping.
Parse and populate '_time' from the syslog header timestamp for every event; CIM compliance requires a structured time field, not just the timestamp embedded in _raw.

Build a complete port-to-application name lookup table covering at minimum: 20/21=ftp, 22=ssh, 23=telnet, 25=smtp, 53=dns, 80=http, 443=https, 445=smb, 3389=rdp, 8080=http — never fall back to the raw port number string as the application value.
Map Check Point 'reason' field directly to CIM 'reason', not to a non-standard 'vendor_info' field; use 'vendor_product' for product names and 'src_user' for authenticated user fields.

For multi-datamodel events (firewall + IPS, firewall + malware), tag appropriately and populate datamodel-specific required fields: IDS events need 'category' and normalized 'severity'; malware events need 'signature' rather than vendor-specific field names like 'malware_name'.
Always extract 'src' (and alias to 'src_ip') from Check Point 'src=' KV field; it is the most critical CIM Network Traffic field and must not be left only in _raw.
Parse syslog timestamps from the log header into '_time' as epoch; CIM requires a numeric _time field on every event.
Maintain a complete port-to-application name lookup table including port 23→telnet, 445→smb, 8080→http; never fall back to the raw port number as the application name.
Normalize vendor severity strings (High, Critical, Medium, Low) to both CIM severity labels and numeric severity scores; use a lookup table.

For multi-model sources (firewall + IPS + anti-malware), branch on the 'product' or 'blade' field and apply the appropriate CIM data model field mappings: Network Traffic for firewall, Intrusion Detection for IPS/SmartDefense, Malware for Anti-Malware events.
Map 'orig'/'product' fields to CIM 'dvc_name' and 'vendor_product' respectively; these are required for device attribution in CIM.
Always extract and convert the syslog timestamp to a numeric epoch _time field — CIM requires _time on every event regardless of datamodel.

For CIM IDS/Intrusion Detection events, map severity strings (low/medium/high/critical) to a proper numeric severity_id (e.g., 1–4) and add tag='ids' and tag='attack' alongside network/communicate tags.
Avoid populating translated NAT fields (src_translated_port/dest_translated_port) by copying the original port when no translated port value exists in the source log; leave the field absent instead.

In CIM, 'service' should reflect the application-layer service name (e.g., 'dns', 'http'), not the raw port number string — use dest_port (integer) for the port and 'application' for the protocol name.
Do not emit both the raw source field and its CIM-mapped equivalent (e.g., user + src_user, dvc + dvc_name) unless the raw field serves a distinct purpose; prefer the CIM canonical name only.
Always extract and populate _time from the syslog timestamp header as a first-priority step; absence of _time breaks CIM compliance and Splunk search functionality.
Remove or rename internal staging fields (e.g., __raw_severity) before final output — empty staging fields should be dropped, not passed through as empty strings.
Do not duplicate layer-4 protocol into both 'transport' (CIM standard) and 'protocol' (non-CIM); choose one per the target datamodel spec.
OCSF-specific numeric fields like severity_id do not belong in CIM output — keep datamodel-specific fields strictly separated.
Validate pipeline serialization completeness — truncated output arrays (as seen in event 8) indicate a buffer, size limit, or regex extraction failure that must be caught in QA.
Always extract and normalize the syslog timestamp into _time (epoch) — even for syslog sources without a year, use the current year or event context.
Use 'protocol' not 'transport' for the network protocol field in CIM Network Traffic; CIM datamodel field names must match exactly.
Do not populate file_name with malware signature names — use 'signature' for malware/attack names and reserve file_name for actual filenames of affected files.
Validate JSON serialization completeness before output — truncated arrays in the last event indicate a pipeline flush or buffer issue that must be caught.

IDS/IPS/Anti-Malware events should map to CIM Intrusion Detection datamodel fields including 'category', 'severity' (normalized), 'signature', and 'ids_type' — ensure all required fields for secondary datamodels are populated when tags indicate a secondary model applies.
Always extract and populate '_time' as an epoch integer from the syslog header timestamp — CIM and Splunk datamodels require it for time-based searches and acceleration.
CIM Network Traffic datamodel uses 'transport' (not 'protocol') for the network protocol, and 'app' (not 'application') for the application layer identifier — use exact CIM field names.

For Check Point logs with multiple product types (Firewall, IPS, Anti-Malware, VPN), apply product-specific CIM datamodel tags and fields: Network_Traffic for firewall, Intrusion_Detection for IPS/SmartDefense, Malware for Anti-Malware, and ensure the 'tag' array reflects the correct CIM datamodel tags.

Preserve vendor original values (e.g., original action, original severity) in vendor_* prefixed fields while normalizing to CIM values, and map 'vendor' and 'product' as separate fields rather than combined 'vendor_product'.
When NAT fields are present (xlatesrc, xlatedst), map both translated IP and translated port to CIM src_translated_ip/src_translated_port and dest_translated_ip/dest_translated_port.
Always extract and parse the syslog timestamp into a CIM _time epoch field; leaving it only in _raw breaks time-based correlation.
Map Check Point 'rule' to CIM 'rule_number', not a bare 'rule' field, as CIM Network Traffic datamodel specifies rule_number.
CIM IDS/Attacks datamodel requires the tag value 'ids-attacks' (single hyphenated string) not separate 'ids' and 'attack' array entries.
For network traffic events, always attempt to populate direction (inbound/outbound) based on RFC-1918 vs public IP heuristics.
Vendor-specific context fields (VPN_peer, VPN_tunnel, malware_name) should be aliased to the nearest CIM equivalent (tunnel_id, signature) in addition to being preserved.
Always extract and emit a normalized _time field from the syslog header timestamp; CIM datamodel acceleration depends on it and its absence is a hard blocker.
Populate host, sourcetype, and eventtype metadata fields in every CIM output event — these are required for Splunk datamodel mapping and pivot functionality.

Direction inference must treat external-source-to-internal-dest as 'inbound' and internal-source-to-external-dest as 'outbound'; RFC-1918 ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) must be used consistently for both src and dst to determine directionality.
For CIM IDS/Attacks datamodel, always include signature_id (even if synthetic) and type alongside signature; for Malware datamodel map malware_name to signature and set appropriate category values.
CIM NAT fields (src_translated_ip, src_translated_port, dest_translated_ip, dest_translated_port) should all be populated when NAT is detected, not just the source translation.
Always extract and populate '_time' as a Unix epoch from the syslog timestamp — CIM compliance requires it and Splunk search depends on it.
CIM Network Traffic datamodel requires bytes_in, bytes_out, packets, and duration fields; populate with 0 or null rather than omitting them when source data lacks them.
signature_id must be a distinct identifier from the signature name — if no numeric ID exists in the source, use a hash or concatenation; never copy the signature name string verbatim.
CIM 'direction' only accepts 'inbound', 'outbound', or 'unknown' — RFC-1918 to RFC-1918 traffic should be 'unknown' or determined by policy context, never 'internal'.

For Check Point VPN events, map VPN_tunnel to 'vpn_tunnel' (CIM VPN datamodel) not 'tunnel_id', and always validate field names against the specific CIM datamodel (Network Traffic vs IDS vs VPN) being targeted.
For CIM Network Traffic, map device IP fields to 'dvc_ip' not 'dvc_id'; reserve 'dvc_id' for device asset identifiers.
Interface names (ifname) should map to 'src_interface'/'dest_interface' in CIM, not 'src_zone' — zones are logical network segments, not physical/logical interfaces.

Omit ECS fields entirely (or use null) when no value is available; never write empty strings to ECS fields like source.nat.ip, user.name, log.level, or threat.technique.name.

Always validate event.outcome against ECS controlled vocabulary: only 'success', 'failure', and 'unknown' are valid — never 'allowed' or 'denied'.

ECS array-type fields like event.type, event.category, and threat.technique.name must always be arrays even when containing a single value; threat.technique.name specifically must be an array of strings.

Normalize proto= values to lowercase consistently and avoid non-standard protocol strings like 'IPv6-ICMP'; use standard CEF values or map to cn2/cs fields with labels.
