aws_cloudtrail::cim: Always map userIdentity.userName (and fallback to principalId for non-IAM types) to the CIM 'user' field — this is the most critical identity field
Map eventName to vendor_action, signature, and signature_id — it is the primary action descriptor in CloudTrail
class_uid and category_uid must be numeric integers per OCSF/CIM spec; use a lookup table to convert event category strings to numeric IDs
event_type must be dynamically set from each event's actual eventType field, never hardcoded to a combined multi-value string
Validate event counts between input and output to detect silent event drops caused by pipeline filter or routing logic
app should be derived from eventSource (strip .amazonaws.com suffix if desired); do not leave it empty when the source field exists

Choose one target schema (CIM or OCSF) and apply it consistently — mixing OCSF structural fields (class_uid, category_uid, severity_id) with CIM field names (src_ip, src_user, action) produces an invalid hybrid.
Always map bytes transfer fields: additionalEventData.bytesTransferredIn → bytes_in and bytesTransferredOut → bytes_out are high-value CIM fields present in S3 CloudTrail events.
Map resource identifiers to CIM dest/object fields: requestParameters.bucketName → dest, requestParameters.key → file_name/object, and EC2 instance IDs → dest for compute events.
In CIM, the action field should contain a normalized verb (read, write, delete, create, modify) not an outcome word like 'success'; outcome/result fields serve that purpose separately.
Preserve userAgent → http_user_agent, userIdentity.arn → user_arn, and userIdentity.accessKeyId → src_credential fields as they carry forensic value present in the source.
For CloudTrail, prefer userIdentity.userName over principalId for the CIM 'user' field; fall back to principalId only when userName is absent (e.g., Root or AWSService types).

Always extract service-specific resource identifiers (instanceId for EC2, bucketName for S3) and populate the appropriate CIM field (instance_id, object, dest) from both requestParameters and responseElements.
Omit or conditionally populate optional fields (mfa_used, instance_id) rather than emitting empty strings when the source event type cannot supply them.

Map eventName directly to a CIM 'action' or 'command' field and use a lookup/eval to derive a normalized action category (read/write/delete/login/create) based on the actual operation name rather than hardcoding.
Use readOnly field as an authoritative signal: readOnly=true should map to change_type='read', not 'write'; additionally, ConsoleLogin events belong to the Authentication datamodel, not Change.
Preserve all identity fields: map userIdentity.arn → user_arn, userIdentity.principalId → user_id, userIdentity.accessKeyId → src_user_id or access_key.
Map eventSource → app, awsRegion → dest or aws_region, eventID → event_id, requestID → transaction_id to satisfy CIM traceability requirements.

Extract nested payload fields: requestParameters.bucketName → object, requestParameters.key → file_path/object_path; additionalEventData.bytesTransferredIn/Out → bytes_in/bytes_out; responseElements status → result.
Never hardcode dynamic fields like action or change_type; always derive them from source event properties, with a safe default only as fallback.
Always map additionalEventData.bytesTransferredIn/Out to CIM bytes_in/bytes_out for S3 and other data-transfer events.
Use CIM-standard field names: 'src_user' (not 'user'), 'src_user_id' (not 'user_id') for the Change/Authentication data models.
For resource-creating events (RunInstances, CreateUser), extract the created resource ID from responseElements and populate object_id; do not fall back to the eventSource hostname as 'object'.
eventID and requestID should always be preserved as vendor_eventid/request_id — they are essential for audit correlation.
For S3 events, use the object-level ARN or requestParameters.key for 'object'/'object_id', not just the bucket ARN.
ConsoleLogin events belong to the CIM Authentication data model (action='login', result based on ConsoleLogin response), not the Change data model.
change_type should map 'Delete*' operations to 'delete', not 'write'.
aws_cloudtrail::ocsf: OCSF class_uid, category_uid, type_uid, and activity_id must be dynamically assigned per event type (e.g., ConsoleLogin→3002, S3 file ops→3005 or 6, EC2→infrastructure class); never hardcode a single class across all events from a multi-service source like CloudTrail.

The OCSF 'time' field must be derived from the source event timestamp (eventTime), not a static or processing-time value; use the already-parsed _time epoch or convert eventTime — never use a fixed placeholder.

OCSF mandates structured nested objects: actor.user (with name/uid/type/account), src_endpoint (with ip), metadata (with version/product), and cloud (with provider/region/account_uid) — mapping identity and network fields to flat scalar fields like 'user' and 'src_ip' is structurally non-compliant.
Always map the actual human-readable username (userIdentity.userName) to actor.user.name, not the identity type string — the type belongs in actor.user.type.
Never emit empty-string fields (login_result: '') for events where the concept does not apply; either omit the field or set it to null for non-applicable events.
Always parse and map eventTime to a correct Unix epoch using a proper date parser; never hardcode or carry forward a pipeline processing timestamp into the OCSF time field.

The OCSF actor.user object is mandatory for CloudTrail — map userIdentity.userName→actor.user.name, principalId→actor.user.uid, accountId→actor.user.account.uid, accessKeyId→actor.user.credential_uid, and userIdentity.type→actor.user.type in every event.

Always populate metadata (metadata.uid from eventID, metadata.product.name/vendor_name from eventSource, metadata.version from eventVersion), cloud (cloud.region, cloud.account.uid), src_endpoint.ip (sourceIPAddress), http_request.user_agent (userAgent), and api.operation (eventName) — these are present in virtually every CloudTrail record and are core OCSF fields.
Maintain a per-eventName class_uid mapping table; IAM CreateUser must not be mapped to File System Activity (3005) — use Account Change (3001) or IAM class (6001).

Set default severity_id=1 (Informational) for all CloudTrail events unless there is explicit source data indicating a different severity; do not assign arbitrary elevated severity values without a documented mapping rule.
Always include OCSF string label companions: type_name, class_name, and category_name alongside their _uid counterparts.
Map actor.user.name from userIdentity.userName (not userIdentity.type); map userIdentity.type to actor.user.type; map principalId to actor.user.uid and accessKeyId to actor.user.credential_uid.
api.operation must be populated from eventName; api.service.name from eventSource — these are core OCSF API activity fields and represent the primary action being audited.

Differentiate class_uid by eventType: AwsConsoleSignIn → class_uid=3002 (Authentication), AwsApiCall → class_uid=6003; compute activity_id from eventName semantics (Create/Read/Update/Delete/Other) and set type_uid = class_uid*100 + activity_id.

Never emit an empty object {} for structured OCSF fields (api.service, cloud.account, actor.user.account, resource, http_request, actor.session) when the source carries values for those fields — always populate or omit the field entirely.

Map eventID to metadata.uid, awsRegion to cloud.region, recipientAccountId to cloud.account.uid, resources[] to the OCSF resource array with uid=ARN and type, and userAgent to http_request.user_agent.
Preserve request/response data in api.request.data / api.response.data or an unmapped object so that operationally critical fields like instanceId, bucketName, and key are not silently dropped.
Always map requestParameters to api.request and responseElements to api.response as structured objects — these are the primary data payloads in CloudTrail and must not be left empty.
Map errorCode to api.response.error and errorMessage to api.response.message (and optionally to status_detail) for any event that carries them; these are critical for failure triage.

For AssumedRole identity type, map userIdentity.arn to actor.user.uid_alt, extract the friendly role name from sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName into actor.user.name, and populate actor.session with credential expiration and accessKeyId from responseElements.credentials.
Always map userIdentity.arn to actor.user.uid_alt regardless of identity type so the full ARN is preserved alongside the principalId uid.

Derive resource.uid, resource.name, and resource.type from requestParameters and responseElements based on eventSource (e.g., bucketName for S3, instanceId for EC2, userName for IAM) rather than leaving resource as an empty object.

Apply more granular class_uid mapping: EC2 provisioning events (RunInstances) should map to Virtual Machine Activity (4001), not Authentication (3002); use a lookup table keyed on eventSource+eventName for accurate OCSF class assignment.

Never emit an empty object for api.request, resource, or actor.session if the source contains requestParameters, responseElements, or sessionContext — always map their key sub-fields or omit the parent key entirely to avoid silent data loss.
Map errorCode → api.response.error (or status_detail) and errorMessage → api.response.message explicitly; failure status alone is insufficient for triage without the error string.

Maintain a class_uid lookup table keyed on eventSource+eventName so EC2/S3/STS calls are not lumped into the IAM class (6003); use class 3005 (API Activity) as the default catch-all for non-IAM, non-auth API calls.
For AssumedRole userIdentity, set actor.user.name from sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName and actor.user.uid_alt from userIdentity.arn — never use the raw ARN string as the display name.

Preserve the full userIdentity.arn in actor.user.uid_alt and store readOnly, managementEvent, recipientAccountId, and eventType in unmapped_data or metadata.labels to prevent complete information loss for fields outside the core OCSF schema.
Always map requestParameters → api.request.data and responseElements → api.response.data; these are the primary payload fields in CloudTrail and must not be left as empty objects.
Map errorCode → api.response.error and errorMessage → api.response.error_message for failed events; also propagate these to status_detail so downstream analysts can filter without re-parsing raw.

Build an eventName-to-class_uid/activity_id lookup table: IAM Create*/Delete* → class 3005 Account Change, ConsoleLogin/AssumeRole → class 3002/3001 Authentication, generic API calls → 6003; a single class_uid for all non-login events produces misleading OCSF output.
For AssumedRole userIdentity, always unpack sessionContext.sessionIssuer into actor.session and map the calling ARN to actor.user.uid_alt to preserve the full trust chain.
Do not assign elevated severity_id based solely on HTTP/API failure status without a threat-intel or risk signal; default failed-auth severity should remain informational (1) unless enriched.
office365_management::ocsf: Operation-to-class_uid mapping must be exhaustive: UserLoggedIn/UserLoginFailed → 3002, FileDownloaded/FileUploaded → 3006 File Activity, MailItemsAccessed → 4002 Email Activity, 'Add member to role' → 6001 IAM Account Change, SearchQueryPerformed → a compliance/search class; never default all events to Authentication.

OCSF output must use nested object structure (actor.user.{name,email_addr,type_id}, src_endpoint.{ip,type}, file.{name,path,size}, metadata.{version,product}) — flat string fields like 'user' and 'src_ip' are not valid OCSF.

Array-valued source fields (ExtendedProperties, Folders, ModifiedProperties) must be iterated and their Name/Value pairs extracted to the appropriate typed OCSF sub-objects rather than passed through as raw arrays.
Do not retain original source field names alongside OCSF fields in the final output; produce a clean OCSF document with unmappable source fields placed in a unmapped or raw_data container object.
The metadata object is mandatory in OCSF and must always be populated with at minimum metadata.version, metadata.product.name, and metadata.log_name even when those values are static constants.

OCSF requires event-type-specific class_uid and activity_id: map UserLoggedIn→class 3002/activity 1, FileDownloaded→class 3001/activity Read, FileUploaded→class 3001/activity Create, SendAs→class 9001, Add member to role→class 3005 — never use a single fallback class for all events.
The OCSF 'time' field must be a Unix epoch in milliseconds (not null, not a string); populate it from CreationTime and ensure it is numeric before output.

OCSF mandates a 'metadata' object (metadata.version, metadata.product.name, metadata.log_name) and structured objects for actor (actor.user.name), network endpoint (src_endpoint.ip), and file (file.name, file.size) — flat scalar fields like src_ip, user, file_name do not conform.
severity_id must be numerically consistent with the severity string: 1=Info, 2=Low, 3=Medium, 4=High, 5=Critical — never leave severity_id=0 when severity is explicitly set.

Always extract nested arrays from Office 365 events (ExtendedProperties, AuthenticationDetails, ModifiedProperties, Target) to avoid losing high-value security context like ErrorCode, UserAgent, and target identities.
zscaler_web::cim: ZPA LSS and ZIA logs require separate parsing branches: LSS logs are comma-delimited with positional fields, ZIA web logs are pipe-delimited key=value pairs — a single regex/delimiter cannot handle both.
Event timestamps must be extracted from the raw log header (e.g., 'Tue Oct 16 16:12:41 2018') and parsed into _time; never rely solely on ingest time.
For ZPA LSS, product should be 'ZPA' not 'ZIA'; the log type ('User Status' vs 'User Activity') should drive field mapping since positional fields differ between the two.

All CIM network fields (src, dest, src_port, dest_port, protocol, bytes_in, bytes_out, user, action) must be actively mapped from parsed source fields — falling back to empty/zero is a critical extraction failure.

For ZIA pipe-delimited logs, use key=value extraction to map LOGINNAME→user, CLIENTIP→src, HOST→dest, PROTOCOL→protocol, ACTION→action, REQSIZE→bytes_out, RESPSIZE→bytes_in, APPNAME→app, URLCAT→category.
Ensure the pipeline has working event routing/passthrough before applying field extractions — a misconfigured route or drop condition can silently discard all events.

Zscaler ZPA LSS logs have two distinct sub-formats (User Status = CSV, User Activity = CSV with different field counts) and Zscaler Web uses pipe-key|value pairs; each requires its own regex or delimiter-based extraction rule, and all must be tested against real sample data.

Always verify that at minimum _time and _raw are populated in output before declaring a pipeline functional; an empty output array is the clearest signal that a filter/route condition is rejecting all events upstream of any transform.

When mapping to CIM for Zscaler sources, validate field name alignment: src_user, src_ip, dest, dest_port, action, app, url, http_method, bytes_in, bytes_out, and transport are the core CIM Network/Web fields that should be exercised in unit tests.
Always parse and set _time from the event header timestamp (e.g. 'Tue Oct 16 16:12:41 2018') using strptime before any other processing — never allow _time to default to ingest/processing time.
When splitting CSV-like ZPA LSS fields, strip surrounding quotes from the entire _raw string before field extraction to prevent trailing-quote artifacts corrupting numeric fields like bytes_rx.

Classify ZPA 'User Status' events (ZPN_STATUS_AUTHENTICATED, ZPN_STATUS_DISCONNECTED) as authentication datamodel events (action=success/logoff), not network_traffic; reserve network_traffic for 'User Activity' connection events.
Never alias dest/dest_ip to src/src_ip when no destination is present in the source — leave dest fields empty or omitted rather than copying the source address.

Intermediate extracted fields (e.g. __zs_bytes_rx, __zs_lat, __zs_lon) must be explicitly promoted to their final CIM field names (bytes_in, src_lat, src_lon) before output; validate that the promotion step handles null/parse-error cases.
Always derive _time from the event's own timestamp string (e.g., 'Tue Oct 16 16:12:41 2018'), not from processing time or a default; validate the epoch value before output.
Clean up all intermediate/staging fields (prefixed __zs_, __fmt, etc.) with a final 'clean fields' step before emitting CIM output.

For multi-subtype sources (ZPA Status, ZPA Activity, ZIA Web), build a separate field extraction branch per subtype and ensure CIM fields like url, dest_ip, dest_port, src_port, protocol, app, category, http_method, http_response_code, and user_agent are mapped from whichever subtype contains them.
Promote extracted geo/meta values (src_country, session_id, dvc) from internal fields to CIM field names rather than leaving them only in private-prefix fields.
When a source field is null/absent, omit the CIM field entirely rather than emitting null or empty string, to keep output schema clean.

ZPA LSS logs (User Status and User Activity) are comma-delimited with positional fields — each sub-type has a different field ordering that must be parsed positionally; build separate regex or CSV parsers keyed on the 'User Status' vs 'User Activity' discriminator in the header.

Always extract _time from the log's own timestamp header (e.g. 'Tue Oct 16 16:12:41 2018') using strptime before applying any CIM mapping; never allow pipeline processing time to become the event timestamp.

Zscaler web proxy logs use pipe-delimited key|value pairs (|FIELD|value|) and must be parsed as such — a generic CSV parser will not work; detect format by presence of '|ZSCALER|' prefix and apply a KV/pipe-split parser to extract LOGINNAME→user, CLIENTIP→src, HOST→dest, URL→url, PROTOCOL→protocol, ACTION→action, APPNAME→app, URLCAT→category, RESPCODE, REQSIZE/RESPSIZE→bytes_in/bytes_out.

Map vendor status codes (ZPN_STATUS_AUTHENTICATED, ZPN_STATUS_DISCONNECTED, BRK_MT_TERMINATED, Allowed/Blocked) to CIM action values early in the pipeline using a lookup or conditional; never leave action as a hardcoded 'unknown' when the source carries explicit status.
IP protocol numbers (e.g. '6') must be translated to CIM transport strings ('tcp') using a lookup table, not left as 'unknown'.
juniper_srx::cim: Always derive action from the event subtype: RT_FLOW_SESSION_CREATE → 'allowed', PACKET_DROPPED → 'blocked'; never default to 'unknown' when the event name is explicit.

RT_FLOW events require a dedicated extraction regex for the 'src_ip/src_port->dst_ip/dst_port' pattern, zone pair (trust>untrust), protocol number, and application name — these must not be silently dropped.
Choose one target schema (CIM vs OCSF) and enforce it consistently: CIM does not use class_uid/category_uid; use tag, eventtype, and category per CIM conventions.

Handle malformed/prefixed timestamps (like '<year>2024') with a fallback parser so _time is not set to a future epoch; apply consistent timestamp and log_time fields across all event types in the same pipeline.
Truncated output (dest: '2') signals a serialization/buffer issue that must be caught in pipeline testing before deployment.
Always map to CIM canonical field names: 'dest_ip' not 'dst_ip', 'dest_port' not 'dst_port' — maintain a CIM field name lookup table and enforce it in the final rename step.

Distinguish 'transport' (L4: tcp/udp/icmp) from 'protocol' (application layer: dns/http/ftp) in CIM; for Juniper SRX, derive transport from the protocol field and protocol from the application/app field.
Validate _time epoch against the parsed timestamp string before emitting — a simple sanity check (parsed_date == epoch_to_date(_time)) catches timezone/offset bugs early.
For firewall drop events, prefer action='dropped' over 'blocked' to align with CIM network_traffic model; reserve 'blocked' for explicit policy block actions where the session was tracked.

Avoid mapping firewall 'reason' to both 'rule' and 'signature' — 'rule' should hold policy/ACL names, 'signature' belongs to IDS context; create a separate 'drop_reason' or use 'reason' as a vendor-specific passthrough field.

Syslog messages without a year (BSD syslog RFC 3164) must assume current year or use a configurable reference year — never let strptime default to epoch year 1970 or year 2001; always validate that parsed _time falls within a plausible recent window.

Multi-source syslog pipelines must branch on process/event-tag (RT_FLOW vs KERNEL vs IDP vs SCREEN) to assign the correct CIM datamodel and event_type before field extraction — a single Network_Traffic catch-all misclassifies system and IDS events.

If targeting Splunk CIM, class_uid and category_uid are not standard fields — use the datamodel tag mechanism; if targeting OCSF, class_uid must be a numeric integer (e.g., 4001 for Network Activity), never a string.
Duration strings like '00:04:23' must be parsed and converted to seconds (integer) before mapping to the CIM 'duration' field; leaving them as null after parsing is worse than not extracting at all.

NAT translation fields should be populated only when actual translation occurred (translated address differs from original); when no NAT is present, omit or null the translated fields rather than copying the original values, to avoid false positives in NAT-detection queries.

Avoid emitting empty-string placeholder fields (user:'', signature:'') for CIM fields that have no source value — omit them entirely to prevent downstream field-presence checks from returning false matches.
Always apply regex extraction for the IP/port tuple pattern (e.g., (\S+)/(\d+)->(\S+)/(\d+)) present in RT_FLOW events before emitting any CIM fields.
Map RT_FLOW_SESSION_CREATE→allowed, RT_FLOW_SESSION_DENY→blocked, IDP action=DROP→dropped for the CIM action field; never default all events to 'unknown' when the subtype directly encodes the action.
Parse the event timestamp from the raw syslog header on every event — not just on some — and validate the resulting epoch is plausible before writing _time.

Classify event_type based on process/facility: UI_AUTH_EVENT → authentication; IDP_ATTACK_LOG_EVENT → ids/ips; RT_FLOW → network_traffic. A single hardcoded event_type for all Juniper SRX events is incorrect.

For SESSION_CLOSE events, extract all numeric fields (bytes_sent, bytes_recv, pkts_sent, pkts_recv) from the space-delimited position-based fields before mapping to CIM bytes_in/bytes_out/packets_in/packets_out.
Do not mix OCSF field names (class_uid, category_uid) into a CIM-targeted output — choose one schema and use its canonical field names exclusively.
palo_alto_threat::cim: For PAN-OS THREAT logs, always map ingress (field 18) and egress (field 19) interfaces to src_interface/dest_interface or inbound_interface/outbound_interface in CIM.
Extract dvc_name from both the syslog header hostname token and the device name field late in the CSV; the serial goes to dvc/dvc_id while the hostname goes to dvc_name.
Never emit explicitly null fields in CIM output — either populate them or omit them to avoid schema pollution.
Strip syntactic wrapper characters (parentheses) from ID fields like signature_id so only the bare numeric value is stored.
Map vsys, log_subtype, sequence_number, and log_profile as they carry important context for PAN-OS threat log analysis in CIM Web and IDS datamodels.
Avoid emitting duplicate semantic fields (protocol + transport both = 'tcp'); pick the correct CIM field name ('transport') and omit the alias.

Always strip surrounding parentheses/brackets from numeric ID fields (e.g., threat-id) before assigning to signature_id; setting a field to null when the lookup fails is worse than omitting it — use a fallback or drop the field.
Extract the syslog header hostname (field between timestamp and message body) and map it to dvc_hostname; do not rely solely on the serial number for device identification in CIM.
For Palo Alto THREAT logs, always map the log subtype (position 5: url/virus/spyware/vulnerability) to ids_type, and always populate vendor_product with a static 'Palo Alto Networks' string.
Avoid emitting internal pipeline metadata fields (sourcetype) as CIM event fields; these belong in index-time metadata, not the event payload.
palo_alto_traffic::cim: For PAN-OS TRAFFIC logs, 'dvc' must be populated from the syslog header hostname (PA-220), not the serial number field — serial number belongs in a vendor-extension field like 'serial_number'.
Always map PAN-OS 'dest_country' and 'session_end_reason' (tcp-fin/aged-out) columns — they are present in every TRAFFIC log and map directly to CIM 'dest_country' and 'flow_action'.

Do not duplicate protocol information as both 'protocol' and 'transport' — Splunk CIM Network Traffic uses 'transport' as the canonical field; 'protocol' is not a standard CIM field in this data model.

Validate NAT port column indices carefully: PAN-OS TRAFFIC col 25 = nat_src_port, col 26 = nat_dst_port; these must be cross-checked against actual column positions to avoid swapped src/dest translated ports.
session_id from PAN-OS should be cast to integer to conform to CIM type expectations.
For PAN-OS TRAFFIC CIM mapping, always map the syslog hostname token (field before the CSV) to dvc_name/dvc_hostname separately from the serial number (dvc/dvc_id).
Map PAN-OS 'url_category_list' (category column) to CIM 'url_category', not a generic 'category' field — non-standard field names break datamodel acceleration.

Always map PAN-OS session_end_reason, ingress/egress interface, and session sequence number — these are present in every TRAFFIC log and have CIM equivalents (end_reason, src_interface, dest_interface).

Validate NAT field mapping by checking whether translated IPs/ports actually differ from original values; if dest_translated_ip always equals dest, the mapping logic is likely copying the wrong PAN-OS column.
Store session_id as a numeric type when the source value is always numeric to maintain consistency with CIM datamodel expectations.
linux_audit::cim: Always map the source's own timestamp field (here 'timestamp' in milliseconds → divide by 1000 for _time) rather than using pipeline processing time.
The 'action' field must be derived from the source event's action/actionType fields, not hardcoded to 'unknown'; implement a lookup or direct mapping.
All primary CIM authentication/change fields (user, src, app, status, signature, object_category) must be explicitly mapped from source fields before declaring a CIM transformation complete.
Source type labeling should match actual log origin — mislabeling as 'linux_audit' when data is CyberArk IDP will cause incorrect downstream parsing and field extractions.
When ingesting structured JSON logs, extract top-level fields (username, userId, source, action, auditType, auditCode, serviceName, message) as CIM fields — do not leave them only in _raw.
Always map the source timestamp field to _time first — for millisecond epoch timestamps (like 1770080106394), divide by 1000 before assigning to _time; never fall back to processing time.
The 'action' CIM field must be populated from the actual source action/event field, not defaulted to 'unknown'; implement auditCode/action-to-CIM-action mapping logic.

Before applying a pipeline, validate that the source format matches the declared sourcetype — CyberArk IDP JSON logs share no structural similarity with linux_audit syslog and require a completely different field extraction strategy.

Core CIM authentication/change fields (user, src, app, session_id, signature, status) must all be explicitly mapped from source fields; a pipeline that outputs only _raw + wrong action is functionally equivalent to no transformation.
Always map the event's own timestamp field (e.g., 'timestamp' in milliseconds → divide by 1000 for _time) rather than using pipeline ingestion time.
Never hardcode CIM 'action' to 'unknown' when the source carries an explicit action field — map input.action directly and reserve 'unknown' only as a fallback when the field is truly absent.

Before building field mappings, verify the actual source schema matches the declared sourcetype; CyberArk IDP audit logs require their own field-to-CIM mapping (user, src, app, signature_id) distinct from linux_audit mappings.

A CIM transformation must extract at minimum: _time (from source timestamp), action, user/src_user, src, app, and signature/signature_id from whichever source fields carry those semantics — outputting only _raw + one hardcoded field is a near-total mapping failure.
Always parse and map the event's native timestamp field (here: 'timestamp' in milliseconds → divide by 1000 for _time) instead of using processing/ingest time.
Map the input 'action' field directly to CIM 'action' rather than defaulting to 'unknown'; only fall back to 'unknown' when the source field is genuinely absent.

Ensure all key identity/network CIM fields (user, src, dest, app) are explicitly extracted from source fields before the pipeline finalizes — a CIM output with only _raw and action=unknown provides near-zero analytical value.
Validate source labeling: if the data does not contain linux_audit-style fields (syscall, auid, pid, key), do not tag it as linux_audit; use the correct sourcetype to avoid downstream confusion.
linux_syslog::cim: Always parse the explicit ISO8601 timestamp embedded in the beat log line (e.g., 2021-06-09T16:17:49.438Z) for _time rather than relying on a fallback that produces incorrect epoch values.
Map the syslog header host field to dvc and the process/program name field to app — these are present in every RFC 3164 syslog event and are core CIM fields.
CIM/OCSF class_uid and category_uid must be integers, not human-readable label strings; define a lookup or constant mapping from event class to numeric uid.
Do not hardcode transport='tcp' or action='success' for events that carry no network or outcome signal — only populate these fields when the source event actually contains that information.
Validate pipeline output JSON is complete and well-formed before scoring; truncated JSON in output events indicates a serialization or field-length bug that must be caught in testing.

Always parse the syslog header to extract host→dvc, process-name→app, and timestamp→_time; the embedded ISO8601 timestamp (2021-06-09T16:17:49.438Z) is even more precise and should be preferred over the syslog header date.
For tab-delimited internal log formats (e.g. beats), split on #011 to extract level→severity, component→process, file→message_id, and message text→signature before mapping to CIM fields.
Use regex on the message body to extract network artifacts (IP→dest, port→dest_port) and derive action from log level/message content (ERROR + 'connection refused' → action=failure, not success).
Numeric CIM/OCSF typed fields (class_uid, category_uid, severity_id) must be integers, not strings; coerce them explicitly in the pipeline.

When mapping linux_syslog metricbeat logs to CIM, parse the #011-delimited fields individually: field[0]=timestamp, field[1]=level, field[2]=component/logger, field[3]=source_file, field[4]=message; signature should be only field[4], not everything after the level.

Always run a secondary regex pass to extract dest/dest_port from error messages containing patterns like 'dial tcp <ip>:<port>' or URLs like 'https://<ip>:<port>' before mapping to CIM dest/dest_port.

Do not emit OCSF numeric IDs (class_uid, category_uid) in a Splunk CIM target schema; CIM uses named fields like 'sourcetype', 'source', 'action', 'vendor_product' — keep the schema vocabulary consistent with the declared target.
Decode literal tab-escape sequences (#011) before assigning to CIM fields, and do not duplicate the syslog hostname in both dvc and src unless there is a distinct network source.
Always parse the syslog PRI+header to extract host→dvc, process/app name→app, and derive the correct epoch _time from the syslog timestamp or embedded ISO8601 timestamp — never use ingestion time.
For Beats log lines, parse the tab-delimited (#011) fields to extract: log level→severity, component→signature, and the free-text message body for dest/url/dest_port using regex.

Do not conflate CIM and OCSF schemas — CIM uses string field names (app, dest, src, action, severity) without numeric class_uid/category_uid identifiers; pick one target schema and apply it consistently.
action and severity_id must be derived from parsed content (log level, message keywords like 'Failed'/'refused' vs 'Attempting'/'success') rather than hardcoded to a single value for all events.
Always parse the syslog PRI+header timestamp first and set _time from it; fall back to any embedded ISO8601 timestamp in the message body. Never leave _time as ingestion/processing time.
Extract standard syslog header fields (hostname → host/dvc, process name → app/process) before any downstream field mapping.

For tab-delimited structured log payloads embedded inside syslog messages (e.g., metricbeat using #011 as separator), apply a secondary parse step to extract log_level, logger, source_file, and message body into dedicated CIM fields.
Severity should be dynamically derived from the parsed log level or syslog PRI severity bits — not hardcoded — so that ERROR events are not misclassified as 'low'.
Network indicators (IPs, ports) appearing in error messages should be regex-extracted and mapped to dest/dest_port CIM fields even when the event is an application log rather than a network flow.
Always decode #011 (and other syslog escape sequences) before assigning to message/signature; the message field should contain only the human-readable description, not appended JSON blobs.

For syslog sources with structured log lines, extract all discrete sub-fields (component/channel in brackets, source file:line, log-level, and message body) into separate CIM-mapped fields rather than leaving them concatenated.
When the log body contains IP:port patterns (especially in error/connection messages), always attempt regex extraction and populate CIM src, dest, dest_port fields accordingly.
Do not reuse message_id for source file references; either create a custom field (log_source_file) or map to an accepted CIM extension field, and document the non-standard usage.
Extract syslog priority into both facility (numeric/name) and syslog_severity (numeric) to fully honour the CIM syslog data model.
aws_vpc_flow::cim: For OCSF-structured VPC flow logs, all network CIM fields must be extracted from nested paths: src from src_endpoint.ip, dest from dst_endpoint.ip, src_port/dest_port from src_endpoint.port/dst_endpoint.port, transport by mapping protocol_num (6→tcp, 17→udp), bytes/packets from traffic.bytes/traffic.packets.
Always map action and disposition fields from the OCSF action/disposition fields to CIM action/vendor_action; never leave these empty as they are core security-relevant fields.
Compute duration as (end_time_dt - start_time_dt)/1000 in seconds, and set _time from the event's own time field (time/1000 for ms epoch), not from ingestion metadata.
When building a CIM output skeleton, validate every field with a non-zero/non-empty default against the source to ensure extraction expressions are actually evaluated before shipping the pipeline.
For OCSF-formatted VPC Flow logs, all network fields are nested (e.g. src_endpoint.ip, traffic.bytes) — use JSON path extraction, not top-level field references.
Always derive _time from the event's own 'time' field (dividing milliseconds by 1000 if needed) rather than the ingest _time field.
Map connection_info.protocol_num to a human-readable transport (6→tcp, 17→udp) before placing in the CIM 'transport' field; do not leave it blank.
Duration should be computed as (end_time_dt - start_time_dt) / 1000 when both epoch-ms timestamps are present in the source.
Default zero/empty values for numeric and string CIM fields indicate the extraction expressions never matched — always test with at least one sample event before deploying.

When the source is nested JSON (OCSF format), all field extraction must use dot-notation paths (e.g. src_endpoint.ip → src, traffic.bytes → bytes); a pipeline that only sets top-level metadata fields without parsing the nested structure will produce empty/zero CIM fields.
Protocol number-to-name conversion must be implemented explicitly: connection_info.protocol_num=6 → transport='tcp', 17 → 'udp'; never leave transport empty when protocol_num is present.

Event timestamps in milliseconds (time=1732753983000) must be converted to seconds (divide by 1000) before assigning to _time; using the ingest/collection _time instead of the event time field is a critical timestamp error.
Duration should be computed from end_time_dt minus start_time_dt (in ms, divide by 1000 for seconds) whenever both boundary timestamps are present in the source.

Always validate that numeric source fields (bytes, packets, ports, severity_id) produce non-zero output values; a zero result for a field whose source value is non-zero is a reliable signal that field extraction is broken.
palo_alto_traffic::ocsf: Parse all CSV fields by positional index for PAN-OS traffic logs — fields like policy_name (12), app (15), zones (16-17), interfaces (18-19), flags (27), action (28), packets (29-30), elapsed (34), end_reason (38), and country (41) must be explicitly extracted.
Always map the firewall action field to OCSF disposition_id/disposition (allow=1, deny=2) as it is a first-class OCSF field for network activity events.
Populate device.name and device.uid from the hostname and serial number in the PAN-OS log header; never emit device as an empty object when source data is available.
Include all OCSF required string label fields (class_name, category_name, type_name) alongside their numeric UID counterparts — UIDs alone do not satisfy the schema.
Map NAT-translated addresses (post-NAT src/dst) to nat_src_endpoint and nat_dst_endpoint objects rather than discarding them.
For session-based traffic logs, always map session start time to start_time, elapsed to duration, and end_reason to connection_info.boundary or an unmapped enrichment field.
For Palo Alto TRAFFIC logs, always map the 'action' field (allow/deny) to OCSF disposition and activity_id — this is the most critical security-relevant field for a firewall log.

Map all CSV positional fields systematically: application (col 9), policy_name (col 6), session_id (col 25), start_time (col 29), elapsed (col 30), pkts_sent/received (cols 33-34), end_reason (col 37), zones, interfaces, and NAT addresses before releasing the pipeline.
Never emit empty objects (actor.user: {}, device: {}) — either populate them or omit them; device.name should always be populated from the syslog hostname or serial number field.
NAT translations (nat_src_ip/nat_dst_ip/nat_src_port/nat_dst_port) are distinct fields in PAN-OS CSV and should be preserved in OCSF as separate nat_* sub-fields within src_endpoint/dst_endpoint.

URL/application category and destination country are always present in PAN-OS TRAFFIC and should be mapped to OCSF enrichment fields (category_name on the network connection, or dst_endpoint.location).
palo_alto_threat::ocsf: For palo_alto_threat OCSF mapping, always parse and map the action field (block-url/allow/drop) to OCSF action_id; severity strings like 'informational/low/medium/high/critical' must be mapped to OCSF severity_id numeric values and never left null.

THREAT/url logs require URL extraction into http_request.url or url_info.url and threat category/ID into threat_name/threat_id — these are the primary indicators distinguishing a threat log from a plain traffic log.

NAT IPs and ports (fields 9,10,26,27 in PAN-OS CSV), zone names, interface names, device serial/hostname, policy name, and application must all be extracted and placed in their corresponding OCSF subobject fields (src_endpoint.nat_ip, dst_endpoint.nat_ip, device.name, etc.); empty skeleton objects like traffic:{} and device:{} indicate the pipeline is scaffolding fields it never populates.

Choose the correct OCSF class_uid for the log subtype: PAN-OS THREAT logs should map to a detection or network-security class (e.g. 4002) rather than generic Network Activity (4001), and type_uid must be derived consistently from the correct class_uid and activity_id.

Palo Alto THREAT logs carry a rich CSV payload — always parse all positional fields (especially fields 11–45+) and map threat-specific fields: action (field 29), severity (field 34), threat name/ID (fields 35–36), app (field 14), rule (field 11), zones (fields 16–17), interfaces (fields 18–19), and URL (field 30).

severity_id must never be null when the source contains a severity string; build a lookup table mapping PAN-OS severity strings ('informational'→1, 'low'→2, 'medium'→3, 'high'→4, 'critical'→5) to OCSF integer severity_id.
Empty OCSF sub-objects (traffic:{}, actor:{user:{}}, device:{}) should either be populated or omitted; leaving them empty signals a broken mapping stage and wastes schema structure.

For URL filtering/threat events, the URL field must be extracted into the appropriate OCSF container (e.g., url.url_string or http_request.url) — it is the primary indicator of the detected threat and its absence is a critical gap.

Device identity fields (serial number, hostname) from PAN-OS logs must be mapped into device.uid and device.name/hostname; the serial number is in CSV field 3 and the hostname appears in both the syslog header and a later CSV field.

For PAN-OS THREAT logs, always map the action field (block-url → action='Denied', action_id=2) and the severity field (informational/low/medium/high/critical → OCSF severity_id 1-6); these are critical for threat classification.
THREAT/url logs must extract the URL and URL category into http_request.url / network_url_category or equivalent OCSF fields — this is the primary indicator of the event.

Zone names, interface names, policy/rule names, session IDs, application name, and NAT addresses are all present in PAN-OS CSV fields and should be mapped to corresponding OCSF endpoint, connection_info, and firewall_rule sub-objects rather than discarded.
Never emit severity_id=null when the source explicitly contains a severity string; build a lookup table (informational→1, low→2, medium→3, high→4, critical→5) as part of the pipeline.
device object should always be populated with the firewall hostname (syslog header field) and serial number (CSV field 3) for PAN-OS sources.
For PAN-OS THREAT logs, always map the action field (block-url, allow, etc.) to OCSF action/action_id — this is one of the most critical security-relevant fields.
URL-type threat logs must extract the URL value into http_request.url or an equivalent OCSF url object; this is the primary observable for this log subtype.
Device identity fields (serial number, hostname) must populate the device object — never emit an empty device: {} when the source carries serial and hostname.

severity_id must never be null when the source carries a severity string; maintain a lookup table mapping PAN-OS severity strings (informational, low, medium, high, critical) to OCSF severity_id integers.
NAT addresses (both src and dst pre/post NAT) are distinct fields in PAN-OS CSV logs and should be mapped to OCSF nat_src_endpoint and nat_dst_endpoint objects.
Zone names, interface names, application name, rule/policy name, and URL category are all consistently present in PAN-OS THREAT logs and should each have explicit OCSF target field mappings.
For PAN-OS THREAT/url subtype, consider OCSF class 4002 (Web Resource Access Activity) over generic 4001 Network Activity to better reflect the semantic of the event.
Always parse the log timestamp field (field 6 in PAN-OS CSV) and map it to OCSF `time` as epoch milliseconds; never leave `time` null or use pipeline ingestion time.

In PAN-OS THREAT logs the CSV field order is fixed: field 7=src_ip, field 8=dst_ip, field 25=src_port, field 26=dst_port, field 29=transport_protocol, field 30=action — verify field indices carefully and never conflate action with protocol_name.

Threat name (field 33) and threat description (field 34) are the core payload of threat logs and must be mapped to OCSF finding/attacks fields; populating empty objects for these is a critical failure.
OCSF severity_id scale: 0=Unknown,1=Informational,2=Low,3=Medium,4=High,5=Critical,6=Fatal — map PAN-OS severity strings accordingly: critical→5, high→4, medium→3, low→2, informational→1.
connection_info.protocol_name must carry the transport layer protocol (tcp/udp), not the firewall disposition; create a separate OCSF disposition_id or action field for the firewall action.
aws_vpc_flow::ocsf: When the source is already OCSF-structured, the pipeline should pass through all existing OCSF fields rather than reconstructing from scratch; a passthrough with targeted enrichment/normalization is far safer than a rebuild.
Always map event time from the source's own time/time_dt field, not from the Cribl-injected _time (ingest timestamp); these can differ by minutes or more.
activity_id, type_uid, action_id, and disposition must be read from the source event dynamically — hardcoding defaults (0, 400100) destroys event classification and makes triage/routing impossible.

Nested OCSF objects (src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, connection_info, traffic, cloud, metadata, observables) must be explicitly preserved or copied; pipelines that only map scalar top-level fields will silently drop all nested context.
Use OCSF-standard field names (type_name, class_name, severity) rather than inventing aliases (event_type) to ensure downstream OCSF consumers and detection rules work correctly.

When the source is already OCSF-structured, the pipeline should pass through all existing OCSF fields directly rather than reconstructing from scratch — a passthrough/reshape approach avoids wholesale data loss.
activity_id and type_uid must be read from the source event, not hardcoded; hardcoding to 0/400100 loses semantic meaning (Traffic vs. Refuse) and produces invalid OCSF events.
Timestamp mapping must use the event's own 'time' field (epoch ms of the flow) not the Cribl ingest '_time' field, which represents pipeline processing time and is unrelated to the event.

Nested OCSF objects (src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, connection_info, traffic, metadata, cloud, observables, unmapped) must each be explicitly preserved or remapped; silently dropping nested objects is the most common cause of catastrophic score loss on pre-structured OCSF sources.
Non-standard field names like 'event_type' should not be invented; use the canonical OCSF field names (class_name, type_name) as defined in the schema.
linux_syslog::ocsf: Always parse and convert the event timestamp from the source (syslog header date or embedded ISO timestamp) to Unix epoch — never use ingestion/processing time as the event time.
Extract syslog header fields (hostname, app/process name) before applying OCSF mapping; map hostname → device.hostname or src_endpoint.hostname and process name → process.name or app_name.

Apply conditional class and severity mapping based on actual parsed fields: map beat log level (INFO→severity_id=1, WARN→2, ERROR→3) and select OCSF class based on message content (network error → 4001, application log → 6001/generic), rather than a single hardcoded class for all events.
Always populate the OCSF 'message' (or 'raw_data') field with the parsed log message body so that the human-readable content is preserved in the output.
For network-related log messages, extract IP addresses and ports using regex and map them to dst_endpoint.ip and dst_endpoint.port within the OCSF network activity object.
Always include an OCSF 'metadata' object with at minimum metadata.version and metadata.product.name to produce a schema-valid OCSF event.
Always extract and map the syslog timestamp (both PRI header date and embedded ISO8601 timestamp) to the OCSF `time` field as a correct Unix epoch; validate the year before shipping.
The log message body (everything after the syslog header) must be mapped to `message` or `raw_data`; dropping it constitutes near-total information loss.
Derive severity_id dynamically from the embedded log level token (INFO→1, ERROR→4/5) rather than hardcoding a single value; apply conditional logic in the pipeline.
Always map syslog hostname to `device.hostname` and process name to `process.name` — these are present in every syslog event and are trivial to extract with a regex.

OCSF class_uid assignment must be content-driven: metricbeat application logs are not Network Activity (4001); use System Activity (1001) or Application Lifecycle (6002) unless confirmed network flow data is present.
Populate the required `metadata` object (version, product.name, log_name) in every OCSF output event.
For events containing IP:port strings, extract them into `src_endpoint`/`dst_endpoint` sub-objects with `.ip` and `.port` fields before assigning a network-class class_uid.
Always parse the syslog PRI, timestamp (both header and embedded ISO8601), hostname, app-name, and message body as distinct extraction steps before OCSF mapping — none of these should be implicit.
Map log-level tokens (INFO, ERROR, WARN, DEBUG) from the message body to OCSF severity_id using an explicit lookup table; never hardcode a single severity for all events.
Validate _time against the source event timestamp during pipeline development — identical _time across all events and a future-date epoch are clear signals that timestamp parsing failed entirely.

Do not blindly assign class_uid 4001 (Network Activity) to syslog application messages; use the message content to select the appropriate OCSF class, or fall back to a generic/unknown class rather than a semantically wrong one.

Empty skeleton objects (src_endpoint:{}, dst_endpoint:{}, traffic:{}, actor:{user:{}}) should only be emitted when at least one sub-field is populated; otherwise omit them to avoid misleading consumers.

Always parse the syslog timestamp (and prefer the higher-precision internal timestamp like '2021-06-09T16:17:49.438Z' when present) to set _time correctly; never leave _time as a processing-time default.
Extract and map the syslog app_name field (e.g. 'metricbeat') to actor.process.name or metadata.product.name rather than hardcoding a generic 'Syslog' label.

Do not include empty OCSF sub-objects (src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, traffic, connection_info) for log classes that are not network events — choose the appropriate class_uid based on the actual event content and only populate relevant objects.
Always map the message body to the OCSF 'message' field; losing the log message text means the entire semantic content of the event is discarded.
Use the extracted log level (INFO/ERROR) to drive severity_id mapping rather than hardcoding a single value across all events.

Always validate timestamp year resolution: syslog lacks a year field, so the pipeline must infer it correctly (current year or rollover logic) — off-by-decade errors corrupt all downstream time-based queries.

Use process name/application token (e.g., 'sshd', 'sudo', 'cron') to branch into the correct OCSF class_uid (Authentication=3002, Scheduled Job Activity=4005, etc.) rather than assigning a single class to all syslog events.
Extract process.name and process.pid from the standard syslog 'program[pid]:' field before message-specific parsing — this applies to every syslog event.

For sshd 'Failed password' events, always populate status_id=2 (Failure) and map the target username and source IP/port; for sudo events map TTY, PWD, target USER, and COMMAND into appropriate OCSF fields.

Remove or populate empty placeholder objects (src_endpoint: {}, dst_endpoint: {}, connection_info: {}, traffic: {}); emitting empty objects wastes space and confuses consumers — only include objects when at least one child field has a value.
Preserve the original raw syslog message in the OCSF 'message' field (or unmapped container) so analysts can always fall back to the source text.
apache_access::cim: Always apply a regex or grok parser for the Apache Combined Log Format before any field mapping; the bracket-enclosed timestamp, quoted request line, status code, bytes, referrer, and user-agent are all mandatory extractions.
Parse and convert _time from the log's own timestamp field (strptime '[%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z]') — never let it default to pipeline-ingestion time.

Map CIM Web data model fields explicitly: src_ip, http_method, uri_path, status (numeric), bytes_out, http_user_agent, http_referrer, and derive 'action' from the status code range (2xx=success, 3xx=redirect, 4xx/5xx=failure/blocked).
Do not hardcode 'action=unknown'; use a conditional (e.g., if status < 400 then 'success', if status == 403 then 'blocked', else 'failure') to make the field meaningful.
Validate that every distinct log field visible in sample input events has a corresponding mapped output field before declaring a pipeline complete.

Always parse the timestamp from the raw log field (e.g., Apache's [dd/Mon/yyyy:HH:MM:SS ±ZZZZ] bracket format) using strptime and assign it to _time; never rely on ingest time when the source carries its own timestamp.

For Apache Combined Log Format, use a regex or grok pattern to extract all standard fields simultaneously: client_ip, ident, auth_user, timestamp, method, uri, protocol, status, bytes, referrer, user_agent — each must be mapped to its CIM counterpart (src, user, _time, http_method, url, status, bytes, http_referrer, http_user_agent).
The CIM 'action' field for web/HTTP data should be derived from the HTTP status code (2xx/3xx → allowed; 4xx/5xx → blocked or error), not left as a static 'unknown'.
Validate pipeline output per-event, not just structurally — identical _time values across events with different log timestamps is a clear signal that timestamp parsing failed.
crowdstrike_falcon::cim: Always map LocalPort → src_port as a numeric integer; never default to 0 when the source field is present and non-empty.
Always map ContextProcessId → process_id (or pid); an empty string is not acceptable when the source value exists.
Decode ConnectionDirection lookup table (0=outbound, 1=inbound) before mapping to CIM 'direction' field rather than defaulting to 'unknown'.
Resolve Protocol numeric values to CIM 'transport' string field (6→tcp, 17→udp) and drop non-CIM intermediate fields like protocol_num.
Do not introduce OCSF-style fields (class_uid, category_uid as strings) into a CIM-targeted pipeline; pick one schema convention and apply it consistently.
Avoid creating duplicate port fields (dst_port vs dest_port); CIM canonical names are src_port and dest_port — use those exclusively.
When mapping LocalPort/RemotePort from CrowdStrike events, always cast to integer and assign to both src_port (CIM) and dst_port/dest_port — never leave as null if the source field is present.
ContextProcessId must be parsed from the JSON payload and mapped to process_id as an integer; avoid using JavaScript 'undefined' as a sentinel — use null or omit the field.
Protocol field '6'→'tcp' translation must populate the CIM 'transport' field (lowercase string), not left as 'undefined'; a simple lookup table (6→tcp, 17→udp, 1→icmp) covers most cases.
Choose one schema target (Splunk CIM or OCSF) and apply it consistently — do not mix OCSF numeric uid conventions with CIM field names in the same output event.
Validate all mapped fields post-transform: any field containing the string 'undefined' or null where the source had a value indicates a broken field reference in the pipeline logic.
Always use 'dest_ip' (not 'dst_ip') for CIM Network Traffic destination IP; CIM field names are exact and case-sensitive.
CIM 'action' must be a disposition value (allowed/blocked/unknown), never an event type name; if no disposition is available from the source, default to 'unknown'.
CIM 'rule_id' should only be populated from an actual rule or policy identifier; tenant/account IDs (cid) must not be mapped to rule_id — use a vendor-specific field or drop it.
Source identifier fields like 'id' (event UUID) should be mapped to CIM 'event_id' to preserve traceability and avoid data loss.
CIM 'dvc' should reflect the originating sensor/host identity (e.g., LocalAddressIP4 or a hostname), not the agent's external/NAT IP (aip).
CIM 'app' for network events should reflect the application protocol (derive from port if necessary, e.g., port 443 → 'https'), never the event type name.
nginx_access::cim: Always parse and map the log timestamp to _time using strptime with the correct format (e.g., %d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z for nginx) before any other transformation.

For nginx access logs targeting CIM Web data model, extract at minimum: src (client IP), http_method, uri_path, status, bytes_out, http_user_agent, http_referrer, dest (upstream), dest_host (vhost), and duration — every field in the combined log line should have a CIM mapping.
Derive action from HTTP status code: 1xx/2xx/3xx → allowed or success; 4xx → blocked or failure; 5xx → error — never leave action as a static 'unknown'.
Use a single Regex Extract or GrokParser function to capture all fields in one pass against the full nginx log pattern, rather than relying on partial extraction that misses most fields.
Validate that _time epoch values fall within a plausible range for the source logs (not a future timestamp or the current processing time).
Always parse and set _time from the log timestamp as the very first pipeline step — null _time renders events nearly useless in any SIEM/CIM context.
Map the last nginx virtual-host field to CIM 'site' explicitly, not just to 'dest_host'; these are separate semantic fields in the CIM Web datamodel.
HTTP status codes must be cast to integers (not strings) and the CIM Web canonical 'url' field should be populated (combining uri_path + any query string from the raw request).

IDP events must be classified under a dedicated intrusion-detection class_uid (not generic Network Activity 4001), and all attack attributes (attack.name, src/dst IPs, ports, severity, action) must be extracted from the structured IDP log fields.

VPN events (KMD_VPN_UP/DOWN) carry operationally critical fields (tunnel name, peer IP, local/remote IDs, gateway, reason) that must be mapped; omitting them renders the OCSF event useless for VPN monitoring.
When parsing syslog timestamps without a year component, default to the current year (not Unix epoch year 2001) to produce a valid and usable _time value.

For Juniper SRX RT_FLOW events, always parse the IP/port tuples from the 'src_ip/src_port->dst_ip/dst_port' pattern and map them to OCSF src_endpoint.{ip,port} and dst_endpoint.{ip,port}; the protocol number immediately preceding the tuple must map to connection_info.protocol_num.
For SESSION_CLOSE events, extract the trailing numeric byte fields (bytes_from_client, bytes_from_server) and map to traffic.bytes_out and traffic.bytes_in respectively.

Source and destination zone tokens (e.g. 'trust untrust') and the policy name inside parentheses (e.g. '5(DEFAULT-PERMIT)') must be extracted consistently across ALL flow event subtypes, not just SESSION_CLOSE.

KMD VPN up/down events are network tunnel events, not authentication events — do not map them to class_uid 3002; use Network Activity (4001) or a VPN-specific class and extract peer IP, tunnel name, local-id, remote-id, gateway, and reason into appropriate OCSF fields.
For UI_LOGIN_* events, always populate user.name from the quoted username token and src_endpoint.ip from the 'from host <ip>' pattern; these are mandatory OCSF Authentication fields.
For IDP events, extract src/dst IP+port from 'from <ip>/<port> to <ip>/<port>' and the action (drop-connection, etc.) into action/action_id; action is a required OCSF field for IDS findings.

Avoid populating both 'message' and 'raw_data' with the identical full syslog string; use raw_data for the verbatim original and either omit message or populate it with a concise human-readable summary.
citrix_netscaler::ocsf: Always parse and convert the syslog timestamp to Unix epoch milliseconds and assign it to both '_time' and the OCSF mandatory 'time' field; a null 'time' is an automatic critical failure.

Always emit 'class_name' and 'type_name' string fields alongside their numeric _uid counterparts, use integer types for ports/timestamps/IDs, and use canonical OCSF enum strings (e.g., 'Informational' not 'informational', 'status_id' not 'action').
For TLS-specific log sources, map all certificate attributes (subject, issuer, serial, validity dates, signature algorithm) into the OCSF 'tls.certificate' sub-object rather than flat custom fields.

Non-OCSF vendor-specific fields (spcb_id, seq_num, node, facility, server_auth) should be placed inside an 'unmapped' object or a declared OCSF extension profile to keep the top-level document schema-compliant.

Every OCSF event must have a valid numeric Unix epoch 'time' field (milliseconds); always parse and convert the syslog timestamp to epoch — leaving it null or as a string string is a critical failure.

OCSF requires a 'metadata' object with 'version' and 'product' on every event, plus string companions for all enum IDs (class_name, type_name, activity_name, category_name, severity label matching OCSF enum not syslog labels).

Non-OCSF vendor-specific fields (spcb_id, seq_id, node, log_type, session_type, handshake_time_ms) must be placed inside an 'unmapped' object or a defined extension, not at the root level of an OCSF event.
Always populate OCSF 'time' as a parsed epoch-millisecond integer — never leave it null; parse the syslog timestamp (e.g. '10/03/2025:15:38:40 GMT') at ingestion time.

OCSF requires nested objects for network endpoints (src_endpoint, dst_endpoint), TLS details (tls object with nested certificate), and connection metadata (connection_info); never flatten these to top-level non-OCSF keys.

Every OCSF event must include a 'metadata' object with at minimum metadata.version and metadata.product (vendor_name + name); omitting it makes the event non-compliant regardless of how well field values are parsed.

All OCSF uid/id integer fields must have their corresponding string label field: class_uid+class_name, category_uid+category_name, activity_id+activity_name, type_uid+type_name, severity_id+severity (using OCSF labels, not syslog labels), status_id+status.

Non-OCSF source fields (spcb_id, facility, node, seq_id, handshake_time_ms) should be placed under 'unmapped' or inside 'metadata.log_name'/'raw_data' rather than scattered at the OCSF event root level.
microsoft_defender::ocsf: Azure Activity Logs are administrative/API audit events — always map to OCSF class 3005 (API Activity) or 6003 (Account Change), never to Process Activity (1007); derive category_uid, type_uid, and activity_id from the correct class.

OCSF requires a metadata object as a mandatory top-level key containing at minimum metadata.version, metadata.product.name, metadata.product.vendor_name — vendor/product as flat fields is not valid OCSF.
Always extract actor.user from identity/claims blocks in Azure logs; the UPN field under identity.claims is the primary user identifier and must map to actor.user.name.
Network/IP source fields must be nested: callerIpAddress → src_endpoint.ip, not flat src_ip.
resultType/statusCode must be mapped to OCSF status (string 'Success'/'Failure') and status_id (integer 1/2); severity string must use OCSF enum label 'Informational' not shorthand 'info'.
When source events are in a records array, ensure the pipeline iterates and emits one output event per record — do not drop subsequent records.

OCSF events MUST be structured as nested objects (metadata, actor, api, cloud, src_endpoint, etc.) — never output a flat field list; define object templates for each mandatory OCSF container before mapping.
The OCSF 'time' field must be an epoch-millisecond integer; always convert ISO timestamps to parseInt(new Date(isoString).getTime()) and never pass through an ISO string or epoch-seconds float.

For Azure Activity Logs, always extract the UPN from the deeply nested path records[].identity.claims['http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2005/05/identity/claims/upn'] — this is the primary user identifier and must be mapped to actor.user.name; leaving it empty is a high-severity data loss.

Every OCSF event requires a 'metadata' object with at minimum metadata.version, metadata.product.name, and metadata.product.vendor_name; add this as a static enrichment step for all Microsoft Defender/Azure sources.

IP addresses must go into src_endpoint.ip (object), not a flat 'src_ip' field; similarly operationName maps to api.operation, not left as a raw copy — always validate target field names against the OCSF field dictionary, not an ad-hoc naming convention.
sophos_xg::ocsf: Sophos XG logs use a key=value syslog format — always apply a KV extraction function (e.g., Cribl's KVParsing function or regex) before attempting field mapping; without parsing, all fields remain in _raw and nothing can be mapped.

Timestamp construction for Sophos XG requires combining date + time + timezone fields and parsing the resulting string; never fall back to processing-time (_time=now) without explicit failure handling.

OCSF class_uid and activity_id must be derived dynamically from log_type and status/subtype fields respectively — use a lookup table or conditional logic: log_type=Firewall→4001, log_type=IDP→4002, log_type=Event/Authentication→3002; status=Allow→activity_id=1, Deny/Drop→2, Alert→4.
OCSF severity_id must be mapped from the source priority field (Information→1, Warning→3, High→4, Critical→5) rather than defaulted to 0.

All network 5-tuple fields (src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port, protocol) are fundamental to OCSF Network Activity and must always be mapped to src_endpoint and dst_endpoint objects as the highest priority fields.
When source events are all identical in output, it indicates the parsing step failed entirely — add validation checks to confirm field extraction before proceeding with mapping.

OCSF requires class_uid to be determined per log_type/log_component: Firewall→4001, IDP/IPS→4003, Anti-Virus→4004, Authentication→3002, Content Filtering→4002; all downstream fields (type_uid, activity_id, category_uid, required sub-objects) depend on correct class_uid selection.

OCSF is a nested-object schema — src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, connection_info, traffic, metadata, actor, malware, attacks, tls must all be constructed as objects/arrays, not left as flat fields; a Cribl eval or serialize step must build these objects explicitly.

Timestamp parsing must be done correctly and stored in _time (Unix epoch) AND metadata.original_time (ISO 8601 with proper UTC offset, not timezone abbreviations); never leave _time null or use a hardcoded pipeline-run time for 'time'.

OCSF integer enum fields (action_id, direction_id, severity_id, activity_id) must be present alongside their string counterparts and must use class-specific enumeration values — a generic mapping table will produce invalid activity_ids across different class_uids.

Sophos XG Anti-Virus events carry file forensics (sha256sum, filename, filetype, filesize, virus name) that must be mapped to OCSF file object and malware array — these are high-value security fields that must not be left as flat strings.

For IDP/signature events, signature_id and signature_msg must be mapped into the OCSF attacks array (technique_uid, technique_name) and the event classified under the correct Finding class, not generic Network Activity.
duo_security::cim: Always parse _time from the event's own timestamp field using strptime/parseTimestamp — never allow it to default to processing/wall-clock time; this is the most critical correctness issue in time-series security analytics.

Canonical CIM fields (user, src, app, dvc, os, src_user) must be explicitly populated from their source counterparts — extracting to custom intermediate fields like user_name without also setting user means CIM-dependent searches and correlation rules will silently miss the data.

Do not mix OCSF schema fields (class_uid, category_uid) into CIM output; choose one target schema and map only to its field names — hybrid outputs break both CIM-based and OCSF-based downstream consumers.

The 'action' field in CIM authentication events should reflect the vendor action type (e.g. 'user_login'), not the outcome/result — result/status already carry the outcome; overwriting action with result destroys event-type information.

When the source 'result' field has a value like 'fraud' that is distinct from 'success'/'failure', preserve it faithfully in the result/status field rather than normalizing it away; also map it to a higher severity tier and do not reassign it to other fields like action or signature.
google_workspace::ocsf: OCSF requires per-event class_uid assignment based on application/event type: login→3002 (Authentication), drive file ops→4001 (File Activity), admin account ops→3005 or 6001 (Account Change), gmail→4009 (Email Activity); never apply a single class to all events.
OCSF 'time' must be a non-null epoch milliseconds integer; never leave it null while populating non-standard timestamp aliases — derive it from the source ISO timestamp during parsing.

All OCSF entities must use canonical nested objects: actor.user{email_addr, uid, name}, src_endpoint{ip}, metadata{version, product{name, vendor_name}}, and class-specific primary objects (file, email, etc.) — flat top-level strings like 'user', 'src_ip' are not OCSF-compliant.

Event parameters arrays from Google Workspace must be extracted and mapped to OCSF fields or placed in unmapped_data/enrichments — silently dropping is_suspicious, doc_title, login_type, target_user, etc. discards high-value security context.

status/status_id are required for Authentication events; severity_id must be numerically consistent with the severity string; activity_id must reflect the specific action per class (Logon vs. Logoff vs. Failed Logon) not defaulted to 1 universally.
OCSF is a deeply nested schema — always emit structured objects (metadata, actor.user, src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, file, etc.) rather than flattening fields with underscore-joined names.
Every OCSF event requires a metadata block with at minimum metadata.version, metadata.product.name, and metadata.product.vendor_name; these must be hardcoded from the known source (Google Workspace).

Map outcome/result to OCSF 'status'+'status_id' (not 'outcome'); map human-readable labels for class_uid→class_name, type_uid→type_name, activity_id→activity_name; ensure severity string and severity_id are always consistent pairs.

Validate class_uid assignments per application: login→3002 (Authentication Audit), admin USER_SETTINGS→6001 (IAM), drive access→4011 (File Hosting Activity) — never reuse a single class_uid for all non-login events.

Never leave unresolved template comments (e.g. 'Authentication / Network Activity based on application_name') in output field values — use conditional logic to resolve to actual OCSF type strings at pipeline build time.
OCSF mandates a 'metadata' envelope object for every event (version, product, log_name, uid) — omitting it makes the event non-conformant regardless of how correct the class_uid is.
User/actor/endpoint context must be OCSF nested objects ({email_addr, uid}, {ip}) not flat scalars; map actor.email → actor.user.email_addr and ipAddress → src_endpoint.ip.

Class assignment must be application-specific: login → 3002, admin CREATE_USER → 3005 (User Account Management), drive file access → 4010 (File System Activity) or equivalent — never use a single fallback class_uid for all non-login events.

Use OCSF-standard status/status_id (1=Success, 2=Failure) not a custom 'outcome' field, and map severity string values to OCSF enum labels exactly (e.g. 'Informational' not 'low', 'Medium' not 'medium').
Never emit pipeline-internal comments or template strings (like 'Authentication / Network Activity based on application_name') as field values in output events.
azure_ad_audit::ocsf: OCSF output requires constructing mandatory nested sub-objects (actor{user{}}, target_user{}, src_endpoint{}, metadata{product{},version}) — never emit these as flat top-level fields.
Map operationType (Add/Update/Delete/Action) to the correct OCSF activity_id per class definition; never default all events to activity_id=1.
The OCSF 'time' field must be a valid Unix epoch in milliseconds derived from the source timestamp — never use a synthetic counter; use _time (already correctly computed) as the source.
Do not duplicate properties sub-fields at the top level; strip raw source fields that have been mapped to OCSF equivalents to avoid schema pollution.

Map targetResources to target_user or target group objects in OCSF; high-value security data like modifiedProperties and ConsentedPermissions must be preserved in a changes[] array or unmapped_data, not silently dropped.

Non-OCSF custom fields (is_high_risk, log_time, action, outcome, event_type, operation_type) must not appear in OCSF output — use OCSF-defined equivalents: risk_score, time, activity_name, status, class_name, activity_id.

OCSF output MUST use nested objects: actor.user (with uid/name/email_addr), metadata (version, product.name/vendor_name), src_endpoint (with ip), and target_user — flat string fields like 'user' and 'src_ip' are not OCSF-conformant.

The OCSF 'time' field must be computed per-event from the source's activityDateTime (or 'time') converted to Unix epoch milliseconds — never use a static/hardcoded value; validate epoch range (2024 events should yield ~1705xxxxxxx ms values).

activity_id, severity_id, and type_uid must be derived from actual event content per-event: map operationType/operationName to activity_id (Create=1, Update=2, Delete=3), resultType to status_id and severity_id (Failure events get higher severity), and type_uid = class_uid*100 + activity_id.

Nested source arrays (targetResources, modifiedProperties, additionalDetails, initiatedBy) must be walked and their values mapped to OCSF structured fields — dropping them wholesale loses the core audit detail that makes these events useful.
ApplicationManagement events should be evaluated for a separate OCSF class_uid rather than forcing all Azure AD audit categories into class 3005 (Account Change).
Always map properties.targetResources[0] to target_user (or app for ApplicationManagement) — this is the most data-rich field in Azure AD audit logs and must never be left as an empty object.

Azure AD audit logs have two identity sources: top-level 'identity' (display only) and properties.initiatedBy.user (canonical, with id/UPN/displayName) — always prefer initiatedBy.user for actor.user fields.

Validate class_uid values against the actual OCSF class registry before publishing; for Azure AD Account Change use class_uid=3001, and derive type_uid as class_uid*100 + activity_id only after confirming the class_uid is valid.

properties.targetResources[].modifiedProperties maps naturally to the OCSF 'changes' array (each entry has displayName->name, oldValue->previous_value, newValue->value) and must not be dropped.
Use OCSF's standard 'unmapped' field name (not 'unmapped_data') and move tenant_id to metadata.tenant_uid to maintain schema compliance.
cyberark_pas::cim: CIM/OCSF class_uid and category_uid MUST be numeric integers — never use descriptive strings; define a lookup table mapping component/event-type to the correct integer codes before output.

Map the source device/host (here 'CyberArk Vault') to the CIM dvc field; do not leave dvc blank when the appliance name is explicitly present in every log line.

Use component-aware event_type mapping: AUTH→authentication, CPM→endpoint/change, PSM→network_session, VAULT→change; a single blanket event_type destroys the semantic value of CIM datamodel separation.

duo_security::ocsf: Always parse the source event timestamp into both _time (Unix epoch float) and the OCSF mandatory 'time' field (epoch milliseconds integer) — never use pipeline processing time for event timestamps.

For OCSF, location data must be nested within src_endpoint.location or user.location as a structured object, not as flat location_city/location_state/location_country fields.
Do not emit empty string values for optional fields like 'reason' when the source value is absent/null; either omit the field or set it to null to keep output clean.

Always map the user/actor object first when processing authentication logs — username is the most critical field for identity events and must appear as user.name (and optionally user object) in OCSF class 3002.
Network source context (src_endpoint.ip, src_endpoint.location) must be extracted from every authentication event; dropping the IP and geo fields makes security analysis impossible.
OCSF requires a metadata object with at minimum metadata.version and metadata.product.name — omitting it produces structurally invalid OCSF output regardless of how well other fields are mapped.
When mapping event types to OCSF activity_id, verify semantics carefully: enrollment is not Logoff (activity_id=2); use a custom or Other activity rather than a semantically wrong standard one.

Non-standard fields (is_external, mfa, result_id, auth_protocol_id) should either be placed in the OCSF unmapped/enrichment object or replaced with proper OCSF constructs rather than added as top-level custom fields.

Parse event timestamps per-event using the source timestamp field; never allow processing-time (_time) to bleed into the OCSF 'time' field — each event must carry its own epoch-millisecond derived from its own timestamp string.

OCSF Authentication (class 3002) mandates status (string) and status_id (integer: 1=Success, 2=Failure, 99=Other) derived from the result field; severity_id must be numerically consistent with the severity string — never hardcode severity_id=1 across all outcomes.
The OCSF user field must be a single object with uid (not key) and name; never emit it as an array or mix object+string — flatten user.key → user.uid at transformation time.
All OCSF events require a metadata object containing at minimum {version, product:{vendor_name, name}, uid}; the txid from Duo logs is the natural metadata.uid candidate.

Differentiate event_type values (authentication vs enrollment vs admin_login) to distinct OCSF class_uid/activity_id combinations rather than collapsing all to class 3002 activity 1.
squid_proxy::cim: Always parse the Squid native log format fields by position (timestamp, elapsed, client_ip, cache_code/status, bytes, method, url, ident, peer/dest_ip, mime_type) before any CIM mapping.
The event's own timestamp field must be extracted and assigned to _time; never let _time default to pipeline processing time.
For CIM Web datamodel, mandatory mapped fields include at minimum: src, dest, http_method, url, status, bytes, action — all derivable from a standard Squid access.log line.

Always parse the Squid access.log with a regex or grok pattern covering all 10 native fields: timestamp, elapsed, client_ip, action/status_code, bytes, method, url, auth_user, peer_type/peer_ip, content_type — before any field mapping.
_time must be set from the first field (Unix epoch, e.g. 1732435200.123) using a numeric cast, never left as processing time.
