Always extract and set _time from the log's own timestamp field (field 1 in Squid native format is a Unix epoch float); never allow _time to default to processing time.

Parse all positional fields from the Squid native log format using a regex or delimited field extractor before emitting: field1=epoch, field2=elapsed, field3=client_ip, field4=cache_result/http_status, field5=bytes, field6=method, field7=url, field8=ident, field9=peer_type/peer_ip, field10=content_type.

squid_proxy::ocsf: Squid proxy logs must be parsed with a regex or delimited parser to extract all 10 native fields before any OCSF mapping; without parsing, all source values are lost.
HTTP proxy traffic should map to OCSF class_uid 4002 (HTTP Activity), category_uid 4 (Network Activity), not Base Event/System Activity.
The event timestamp must be derived from the first field of each source record (Unix epoch, e.g. 1701432888.771 × 1000 for ms), never from processing/wall-clock time, and must be unique per event.

OCSF metadata object (metadata.version, metadata.product.name) must be constructed from source context; bare 'sourcetype' is not a valid OCSF field.
activity_id should reflect the HTTP method: GET → 1, POST → 2, etc., for HTTP Activity class events.

Squid native logs MUST be parsed with a regex or parser that extracts all positional fields: timestamp(ms epoch), elapsed_ms, client_ip, cache_code/http_status, bytes, http_method, url, ident, peer_type/peer_ip, content_type — none can be inferred from the source type alone.
Squid proxy logs map to OCSF class_uid=4002 (HTTP Activity), category_uid=4 (Network Activity), type_uid=400200+; never to Base Event (1001) which carries no network/HTTP semantics.

The event timestamp MUST be converted from the source epoch (field 1, e.g., 1732435200.123 × 1000 → milliseconds) and set as 'time'; using pipeline ingestion time produces identical, wrong timestamps across all events.

For proxy/web logs, URL, src IP, dst IP, HTTP method, and response code are the minimum mandatory fields — a pipeline that omits all of them produces zero analytical value regardless of correct OCSF skeleton fields.

cyberark_pas::ocsf: CyberArk PAS events span multiple OCSF classes: Logon/Logoff → 3002 (Authentication), RetrievePassword → 3005 (File System Activity) or a PAM-specific extension, ChangePassword → 3004 (Account Change), AddSafe/configuration → 3006 (Configuration State Change) — always map source action type to distinct OCSF class_uid.

OCSF is a nested-object schema, not flat key-value: actor.user.name, src_endpoint.ip, dst_endpoint.ip, and metadata.product must be structured objects — never emit user or src_ip as bare top-level strings.
Always populate metadata.version (e.g., '1.1.0') and metadata.product.{name, vendor_name} as they are required OCSF envelope fields present in every compliant event regardless of source.

Non-standard source-specific fields (safe_name, target_account, is_privileged_action) must be placed under an 'unmapped' dictionary object in OCSF rather than at the top level to maintain schema compliance.
Always parse all pipe-delimited positional fields from CyberArk PAS logs before mapping: field 4 = actor username → actor.user.name, field 5 = source IP → src_endpoint.ip — these are never optional.

Every OCSF output event MUST include a metadata object with at minimum metadata.version (e.g., '1.1.0') and metadata.product.name ('CyberArk PAS'); omitting it makes the event schema-invalid regardless of other field quality.

Verify class_uid/category_uid/type_uid values against the published OCSF schema before use; inventing IDs (3005, 3006) or misassigning categories will break downstream OCSF consumers — RetrievePassword should map to class_uid 3003 (Account Change) or a Privileged Activity class, not a non-existent Discovery class.
class_name and type_name are required OCSF string companions to their numeric uid counterparts and must always be emitted alongside class_uid and type_uid.
raw_data should contain the full original log line, not a subset; use the complete pipe-delimited string so analysts can always reconstruct the original event.

Always extract and map all pipe-delimited structured fields (username at position 4, IP at position 5, vault name at position 2) to their OCSF actor.user.name, src_endpoint.ip, and metadata.product.name respectively — these are required by the schema and present in every CyberArk PAS log line.

Every OCSF event requires a 'metadata' top-level object with at minimum metadata.version and metadata.product; failing to emit it makes the output structurally non-compliant regardless of how well other fields are mapped.

RetrievePassword / credential-access actions from CyberArk PAS should not be mapped to OCSF Account Change (3003); prefer class 3005 (Authorize Session) or use class 3002 with a custom activity, and always validate that the activity_id values used actually exist in the chosen class's enum.

For IAM-related events that affect a target account distinct from the actor, extract and populate target.user.name (e.g. WIN-DB01\Administrator for password retrieval) in addition to actor.user.name; both roles are present in CyberArk messages and required by OCSF.
Context-rich fields extracted from free-text messages (safe names, attempt counts) should be mapped to OCSF resources[], unmapped_data, or custom observables rather than discarded.
infoblox_dns::cim: Always extract and map DNS-specific CIM fields: 'query' (domain name), 'query_type' (record type), 'src_port' (client ephemeral port), and 'dest'/'dest_ip' (resolver IP) from Infoblox named logs before considering the transformation complete.

When parsing syslog with no year in the timestamp (e.g., 'Dec 15 00:03:12'), always inject the current or correct year before converting to epoch — defaulting to year 1970 or 2001 is a silent but severe data quality failure.
Never leave severity_id as null when severity is populated; define a numeric mapping table (e.g., informational=1, low=2, medium=3, high=4, critical=5) and apply it consistently.

For Infoblox DNS logs, treat DNS_RPZ events as a distinct high-severity event subtype and map the rewrite target domain to 'dest_dns_name' and the RPZ policy to a dedicated field rather than just elevating severity on the generic signature field.
version.bind TXT queries are a well-known DNS reconnaissance technique and should be mapped to at least medium severity, not informational, to support proper alerting in a CIM-normalized SIEM.
Always parse the syslog header timestamp (MMM DD HH:MM:SS) into _time using strptime; never let _time default to pipeline-execution time.

For Infoblox named DNS logs, use a single regex to capture all named groups in one pass: hostname, process, pid, client_ip, client_port, query_name, query_class, record_type, flags, resolver_ip, and optional response code (NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL).
Map NXDOMAIN and other DNS response codes to a meaningful CIM 'action' value (e.g., 'nxdomain', 'servfail') rather than hardcoding 'unknown' for all events.
CIM DNS fields require at minimum: src_ip, src_port, query (domain), record_type, dest_ip (resolver), dvc, and action — none of these should be left unmapped when the source provides them.
Do not invent non-CIM fields like 'sourcetype' as a CIM output field; CIM target schemas have defined field names that must be used exactly.
microsoft_dns::cim: Microsoft DNS debug logs encode the FQDN in a length-label format like '(4)mail(6)google(3)com(0)' — always decode this into a dot-separated FQDN and map it to CIM 'query' or 'dest_dns_name'.
For DNS CIM, 'app' must be 'dns' (the application protocol), 'transport' carries UDP/TCP, and 'protocol' should also be 'dns' — never copy transport into app.
DNS reply codes (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL) must map to CIM 'reply_code', not to 'action'/'blocked' — NXDOMAIN is a negative DNS response, not a security block event.

Always extract the Q/R flag, record type (A/MX/AAAA/TXT/AXFR/PTR), and transaction ID from DNS logs — these are core discriminators for DNS analytics and threat detection (e.g. AXFR zone transfer attempts, TXT exfiltration).
Never emit explicitly-null CIM fields (severity_id=null); either populate with a valid value or omit the field entirely from the output event.

Always parse the event timestamp into _time as a Unix epoch float per-event; never let a static ingestion time propagate to all events — use a Time extraction function keyed to the log's date/time fields.
For CIM DNS/Network Resolution datamodel, the queried hostname MUST be mapped to the field 'name'; 'query' and 'dest_dns_name' are not CIM-standard and will break CIM-accelerated searches.

Microsoft DNS debug logs embed the packet memory pointer (e.g. 0000000012A3F1C0) separately from the DNS wire transaction ID; map the wire transaction ID to 'transaction_id' but do not discard the pointer — store it as a supplemental field like 'dns_packet_ptr'.

CIM Network Resolution events require both 'src' (querying client) and 'dest' (responding DNS server); when the server identity is not in the log, populate dest from a lookup or pipeline-injected host variable rather than leaving it absent.

Avoid creating redundant non-CIM fields (dest_dns_name, log_time, query_type when record_type suffices, direction) alongside correct CIM fields — they create confusion and bloat without adding CIM compliance.
infoblox_dns::ocsf: For Infoblox DNS → OCSF, always extract and map the QNAME to query_info.hostname and the record type (A/AAAA/MX) to query_info.type — these are the primary DNS payload fields and their absence makes the output nearly useless for DNS analytics.
Parse the resolver IP from the parenthetical at the end of named query lines (e.g., '(10.10.0.1)') and map it to dst_endpoint.ip; this distinguishes which resolver handled the query.

Year-ambiguous syslog timestamps (no year in header) must anchor to the correct year using the ingest context or a configurable reference year — defaulting to epoch 0 or year 2001 is a silent data quality failure that corrupts all time-based analysis.

RPZ/policy block events must be classified with a distinct activity_id (deny/block) and the POLICY and RULE names must be preserved in dedicated OCSF fields (e.g., firewall_rule.name or unmapped extensions); hardcoding activity_id:1 for all events loses security context.
severity_id must never be null in OCSF output — use 0 (Unknown) as the minimum for informational events, and apply higher severity for denied/blocked events; null fails OCSF schema validation.
Omit empty objects (traffic:{}, actor.user:{}) when the source provides no data for them, to avoid schema validation failures and reduce output bloat.

Parse the syslog timestamp first and set _time/time from the event's own timestamp, not the ingest time; use a strptime or date-parsing function keyed on the syslog header before any other transforms.

Extract structured fields with a regex that captures named groups: client_ip, client_port, query_name, query_class, query_type, flags, resolver_ip, and optionally rcode (NXDOMAIN), then map each to the correct OCSF path (src_endpoint.ip, src_endpoint.port, dns.hostname, etc.) before emitting the event.

Never emit empty OCSF sub-objects (src_endpoint:{}, device:{}, traffic:{}, actor.user:{}) — either populate them with at least one field or omit them entirely to avoid schema validation failures and misleading output.

Distinguish product metadata from category labels: metadata.product.name should be the actual product name ('NIOS'/'Infoblox DNS') not the OCSF category name ('Security'), and vendor_name should be the canonical vendor ('Infoblox') not the sourcetype string.
For DNS activity logs always map the NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL response codes to status_id and dns.rcode; these are high-value security signals that must not be silently dropped.
bind_dns::cim: Always parse and convert the log's own timestamp string to epoch for _time — never leave _time as a static processing-time value; BIND uses 'DD-Mon-YYYY HH:MM:SS.mmm' format which must be explicitly parsed.
Map each log severity token (info/warning/error/critical) to the CIM severity field dynamically using a lookup table — never hardcode a default severity for all events.

Do not mix OCSF field names (class_uid, category_uid) into a CIM output; CIM uses 'tag', 'sourcetype', 'index', and datamodel-specific field names like 'query', 'record_type', 'src', 'dest', 'transport'.
In CIM DNS datamodel, the queried domain name belongs in the 'query' field, not 'url' or 'object'; extract it from the parenthesized domain or TXT record name in the raw log.

System/daemon events (SIGHUP reload) are not DNS queries — branch your event classification logic so non-query events get appropriate event_type values and do not inherit network-session fields like dest_port or direction.
snort_ids::cim: Never assign a fabricated 'action' value (e.g., 'blocked') to IDS alert events — IDS sensors detect and alert only; 'blocked' is only valid for IPS/firewall sources. Use 'allowed' or omit the field entirely for pure IDS.
When a log source carries no embedded timestamp, use _time from ingestion metadata but document it; never assign the same static epoch to all events as if it were an event timestamp.
Do not mix OCSF schema field names (class_uid, category_uid as string labels, type_uid) with CIM field names in the same output — choose one target schema and map only to its defined field set.
Eliminate redundant field copies during normalization: if CIM says 'dest', do not also emit 'dst_ip'; if CIM says 'signature_id', do not also emit 'sid', 'rule_id', and 'rule' with identical values.

For Snort IDS logs, the canonical CIM IDS fields are: src, src_port, dest, dest_port, transport, signature, signature_id, severity, category, ids_type='network', vendor_product — map to exactly these and drop non-CIM duplicates.
suricata_ids::cim: When extracting nested fields into intermediate names (alert_action, http_url, etc.), always add a second mapping step that copies those values into canonical CIM field names (action, url, dest, transport, signature, etc.) — extraction without CIM remapping produces no CIM value.
Never overwrite event_type with a static string for all events; preserve or conditionally set it based on the actual source event_type field to maintain event categorization.

dest_port (and all numeric fields) must be sourced from the parsed field, not defaulted to 0; always verify that field references resolve correctly and add a fallback only when the source genuinely lacks the value.

Flow stats (bytes_toserver/toclient, pkts_toserver/toclient) must be explicitly mapped to CIM bytes_in, bytes_out, packets_in, packets_out — the direction convention (toserver=out from src perspective) must be defined and applied consistently.
class_uid and category_uid in OCSF-aligned CIM must be numeric integers, not human-readable strings; maintain a lookup table from event_type to the correct numeric class/category IDs.
snort_ids::ocsf: For Snort IDS alerts, always use OCSF class_uid 4004 (Detection Finding) not 4001 (Network Activity); map severity_id from Snort Priority (1→Critical/5, 2→High/4, 3→Medium/3) not as a flat low/medium/high string.
Always parse and preserve port numbers from IP:port notation in Snort logs; structure them into OCSF endpoint objects: src_endpoint:{ip, port} and dst_endpoint:{ip, port}.
Wrap vendor/product info in a 'metadata' OCSF object; wrap gid/sid/rev into a 'rule' object; wrap protocol into 'connection_info'; flat field names do not satisfy OCSF schema structural requirements.
When source logs lack embedded timestamps, document that _time is ingestion time and verify the resulting epoch value is sane (year 2026 timestamps suggest a system clock or formula error).
osquery_results::ocsf: Always populate OCSF 'time' from the source's unixTime field (not a nested column like start_time); 'time':0 is a critical defect that makes the event unusable for timeline analysis.

OCSF class_uid, category_uid, type_uid, and severity_id must be dynamically assigned per query/event type — use a lookup or conditional branch per query_name rather than a single hardcoded value for all events.
severity_id must be numerically consistent with the severity string (e.g., critical→5, high→4, medium→3, low→2, informational→1); never hardcode severity_id=1 when severity can be 'critical'.

Pack name splitting should use the fixed prefix 'pack_' and split only on the SECOND underscore, or use a regex that captures the full pack name up to the last underscore-separated query segment — simple first-underscore splits break multi-word pack names like 'pack_hardware_info_cpu'.

Map ALL source column values to output fields; use a generic passthrough for unknown columns rather than selectively dropping fields like gid, cpu_subtype, net_namespace, and osquery metadata (counter, epoch).

For network query types (open_sockets, listening_ports), remap to OCSF Network Activity class (4001, category 4) and populate src_endpoint/dst_endpoint objects including port numbers — do not force-fit into Process Activity class.
suricata_ids::ocsf: OCSF is a deeply nested schema — never flatten it. Always produce src_endpoint:{ip,port}, dst_endpoint:{ip,port}, metadata:{version,product:{name,vendor_name}}, and for IDS alerts a finding:{title,rule_uid,desc} object.

Map Suricata event_type to the correct OCSF class_uid: alert→2004 (Detection Finding), dns→4003 (DNS Activity), http→4002 (HTTP Activity), tls→4001 (Network Activity), fileinfo→1001 (File Activity); never use a single class for all event types.
Suricata alert.severity is inverted relative to OCSF severity_id: Suricata 1=highest, OCSF 1=Informational/lowest. Map Suricata 1→OCSF 5 (Critical), 2→4 (High), 3→3 (Medium), 4→2 (Low).
Convert alert.action to OCSF disposition_id enum (1=Allowed, 2=Blocked, etc.) and produce both disposition_id (int) and disposition (string) fields.
Preserve the original Suricata event_type value in a metadata or unmapped field; do not overwrite it with the OCSF class name string.
carbonblack_edr::ocsf: Map Carbon Black EDR event types to distinct OCSF classes: endpoint.event.procstart → class_uid 1007 (Process Activity), endpoint.event.netconn → 4001 (Network Activity), endpoint.event.filemod → 1001 (File System Activity), endpoint.event.regmod → closest available class (e.g., 1010 Kernel Activity or custom); never hardcode a single class_uid for all event types.

OCSF requires nested object construction, not flat fields: always build device{}, actor{user{}, process{}}, file{hashes[]}, src_endpoint{}, dst_endpoint{}, connection_info{}, and metadata{} sub-objects from source fields rather than promoting values to the root event.

Derive type_uid as class_uid * 100 + activity_id only after class_uid and activity_id are correctly determined per event type; similarly derive category_uid from the correct class, not a hardcoded value.

Do not invent pipeline-internal enrichment fields (proc_risk, encoded_command, network_risk) in OCSF output; use OCSF-defined extension points such as unmapped or enrichments if custom data must be preserved.
Validate serialization completeness — truncated output events indicate a pipeline buffer or size limit issue that must be caught and handled before events are forwarded.

OCSF is a deeply nested schema: every transformation must build proper nested objects (actor.process, device, metadata, file, src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, connection_info) — flat field aliasing is insufficient and non-conformant.
Hash values (md5, sha256) must be mapped to an OCSF hashes array with typed objects: [{type_id:1, value:'<md5>'},{type_id:3, value:'<sha256>'}] inside the appropriate process.file or file object.
The metadata object is mandatory in every OCSF event and must include at minimum metadata.version and metadata.product.name; its absence is a structural failure.
Per-event conditional logic must resolve event_type/activity_id to a single value for the specific event being processed — not emit a static concatenation of all possible mappings.

Registry modification events (ingress.event.regmod) should not be mapped to File System Activity (1001); use a vendor extension class or the closest applicable OCSF class with correct activity_id, and always map registry_key/registry_value into a proper reg_key object.
After OCSF mapping, original raw source fields should be removed or moved to unmapped/raw_data to avoid polluting the structured OCSF document with duplicate flat keys.
Always populate OCSF 'time' from the parsed epoch timestamp in milliseconds (multiply _time seconds by 1000); never leave it as 0 or rely on a separate event_time string field.

Map each Carbon Black event type to its correct OCSF class_uid before setting any other class-dependent fields: ingress.event.netconn → 4001 (category 4), ingress.event.process → 1007 (category 1), and derive category_uid and type_uid programmatically from class_uid and activity_id.

Construct OCSF structured objects (metadata, actor, process, src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, file, connection_info) rather than passing source fields through flat; OCSF is an object schema and flat fields will fail validation.

The 'metadata' object is mandatory in every OCSF event — at minimum include metadata.version, metadata.product.name, metadata.product.uid, and metadata.product.vendor_name derived from the sourcetype.

Resolve field name collisions before writing to OCSF slots: if the source has an 'action' field (e.g., regmod createkey), stage it under a temporary name and derive the OCSF 'action' value independently, or place the raw source value in unmapped/extensions.

Do not place pipeline logic or mapping documentation in data fields like event_type; the event_type / type_name field should contain the resolved OCSF type name string for the specific event being processed.
sentinelone_edr::ocsf: OCSF class_uid MUST be determined per event_type before any other mapping: THREAT→2004, PROCESS_CREATION→4007, NETWORK_CONNECTION→4001, FILE_MODIFICATION→1001, POLICY_VIOLATION→6001, AGENT_CONNECT→4001 or 1001 — never hardcode a single class for all events.

All OCSF fields must be placed in the correct nested object hierarchy (metadata, device, actor.user, actor.process, src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, file, finding) — flat vendor fields do not constitute OCSF output regardless of field name.

Enum ID fields (severity_id, activity_id, type_uid, action_id) must be computed integer values, never left at 0/Unknown when the source provides the information to derive them; type_uid = class_uid * 100 + activity_id.
Never write routing-logic documentation strings into field values; event_type or any mapped field must contain only the actual extracted source value.

The metadata object (with product.name, product.vendor_name, version) is mandatory in every OCSF event and must be populated even when the source does not provide it, using known product context (e.g., 'SentinelOne', 'SentinelOne Inc.').
mimecast_email::cim: Always map source field names to their exact CIM equivalents: subject=subject, msgId=message_id, size=bytes, dir=direction — never leave the canonical CIM field empty while populating a custom alias instead.
OCSF/CIM class_uid and category_uid must be numeric integers (e.g., 4009 for email activity), never string labels; validate type constraints before shipping.

Enumerate all source fields at pipeline design time and assert every one has a target mapping or an explicit drop decision — fields like dkim, threatType, threatDetail, policyResult, and dir were silently lost.

Derived boolean/severity fields (auth_failure, severity, severity_id) must be consistently computed from the same logic; severity_id=0 while severity='high' is a contradiction that indicates the derivation was only partially implemented.
When a source provides both envelope and header sender addresses, map the envelope sender (envFrm) to src_user and populate the CIM src field; do not leave core identity fields empty.
aws_guardduty::cim: Always use CIM-canonical destination field names: 'dest_ip', 'dest_port', 'dest_mac' — never 'dst_*' variants, as those are not CIM standard.
Do not mix OCSF schema fields (class_uid, category_uid as numeric/enum) into CIM output; CIM categorization uses eventtype tags and sourcetype, not class_uid strings.
Map the GuardDuty 'blocked' boolean directly to CIM 'action' field: blocked=true → 'blocked', blocked=false → 'allowed'; never invert this.
Use CIM 'direction' (not 'network_direction') for connectionDirection values, and normalize INBOUND→inbound, OUTBOUND→outbound consistently.
Always validate pipeline output JSON is complete and well-formed before scoring; truncated output indicates a serialization bug that must be caught in testing.
kubernetes_audit::cim: Always parse nested annotation objects from Kubernetes audit logs — 'authorization.k8s.io/decision' and 'authorization.k8s.io/reason' are critical security fields that must be extracted with proper dot-notation or escaped key handling.
Map HTTP response codes to CIM 'action' semantically: 2xx = 'success', 4xx/5xx = 'failure'; never hardcode 'success' across all events.

CIM class_uid and category_uid must be numeric integers (e.g., 3002 for API Activity), not human-readable strings — use a lookup table to convert source event types to valid OCSF/CIM numeric identifiers.

Populate CIM canonical fields (src, url, user, src_user, object, subject, session_id) from available source values before creating custom fields like src_ip or request_uri — CIM compliance requires the standard field names to be populated.
For Kubernetes audit logs, always check objectRef.subresource (e.g., 'exec', 'log') as it changes the semantic meaning of the event and should influence severity and operation classification.

When a source field is already extracted into a custom field (e.g., username → username), also populate the canonical CIM alias (user, src_user) — do not leave CIM fields empty just because a non-standard equivalent exists.
mimecast_email::ocsf: Mimecast email logs must map to OCSF class_uid 9001 (Email Activity), category_uid 9, not Network Activity (4001/category 4) — always verify the OCSF class for the source type before building the pipeline.
OCSF 'time' (epoch ms integer) is mandatory and must be populated; never leave it null — if '_time' is computed correctly, assign it to 'time' as well.

OCSF uses deeply nested objects (email{subject, message_uid, size, attachments[]}, src_endpoint{ip}, metadata{version, product{vendor_name}}, malware[{name}]) — flat field names like src_ip, msg_id, virus are non-compliant and will fail schema validation.

severity_id must be kept in sync with the human-readable severity field using the OCSF enum (0=Unknown,1=Info,2=Low,3=Medium,4=High,5=Critical) — hardcoding severity_id=0 while computing severity='critical' is a contradiction.
activity_id must reflect the actual event action per the class definition (e.g., for Email Activity: Send, Receive, Deliver, Reject differ) — do not hardcode a single activity_id across all events.
Comma-separated source fields like AttNames must be split into proper arrays of OCSF typed objects (file objects for attachments) not retained as raw strings.
Auth indicator strings like [SPF_FAIL][DKIM_FAIL] should be parsed into structured OCSF email authentication fields, not just flat booleans disconnected from the OCSF schema.
aws_guardduty::ocsf: Never hardcode class_uid/category_uid/type_uid — derive them from actionType (NETWORK_CONNECTION→4001, AWS_API_CALL→6003) and compute type_uid = class_uid*100 + activity_id dynamically.
severity_id must be derived from the numeric severity score using the OCSF mapping table (0.1-3.9→Low, 4.0-6.9→Medium, 7.0-8.9→High, 9.0-10→Critical); never hardcode it.

For directional network events, always assign src_* fields from the INITIATING party and dst_* from the RECEIVING party — for OUTBOUND the EC2 instance is src, remote is dst; for INBOUND the remote is src, EC2 is dst — geo/ASN must follow the same party as the IP.
OCSF requires a structured metadata object (not flat vendor/product fields) and a finding object; map the ARN to metadata.uid or finding.uid to preserve the canonical identifier.
Do not propagate empty-string field values from the source — use null or omit the field to keep output clean and avoid false 'present but empty' fields in downstream consumers.
kubernetes_audit::ocsf: Map class_uid based on the Kubernetes verb and resource type: write verbs (create/update/patch/delete) on config resources → API Activity (6003); auth failures (401/403 on sensitive resources) → Authentication (3002); read verbs → API Activity or Query.

Always populate OCSF structural objects: actor.user.{name,uid,groups} from user.*, src_endpoint.ip from sourceIPs[0], http_request.{url,method,user_agent} from requestURI/verb/userAgent, and metadata.uid from auditID.
Derive _time from the event's own timestamp (requestReceivedTimestamp parsed to Unix epoch), never from pipeline processing time; verify _time differs across events as a basic sanity check.

Map responseStatus.code to status_code and status_id, and map annotations['authorization.k8s.io/decision'] to a status or authorization field — these are the primary indicators of access control outcome in Kubernetes audit logs.

For Kubernetes audit events with requestObject present, extract security-relevant sub-fields (container images, hostNetwork, hostPID) into OCSF api.request or unmarshal structures rather than passing them through as opaque blobs.

Always parse nested annotation objects (annotations['authorization.k8s.io/decision']) explicitly — dot-notation keys with slashes require special extraction logic in Cribl (use e.g. nested JSON path or rename steps).

OCSF 'time' must be derived from the event's own timestamp field (requestReceivedTimestamp converted to epoch milliseconds), never set to a static/processing-time value; validate with at least two distinct events during testing.
severity_id must be computed consistently with the severity string — use a lookup/eval that maps 'info'→1, 'low'→2, 'medium'→3, 'high'→4 and apply the same logic to both fields in a single step.

OCSF compliance requires nested objects (actor.user, src_endpoint, http_request, cloud, api); flat fields like username or src_ip satisfy no OCSF consumer — use Cribl's Restructure or nested field assignment to build proper sub-objects.

Required OCSF companion fields (activity_name, type_name, class_name, category_name, status, status_id) must all be populated alongside their _uid counterparts — test by validating against the official OCSF schema validator, not just checking uid presence.
vmware_vcenter::ocsf: Map each distinct VMware vCenter event type to its correct OCSF class_uid: authentication events→3002, system/infrastructure events like alarms→1001 or 2001, VM lifecycle tasks→6003 or a custom Infrastructure Change class; never apply a single class_uid to all events.

Always implement OCSF nested object structures: user identity must be under actor.user.{name,uid}, network endpoints under src_endpoint.{ip,hostname} and dst_endpoint.{ip,hostname}, and API details under api.{operation}.

For Authentication class events, status_id (1=Success, 2=Failure) and activity_id (1=Logon, 2=Logoff) are mandatory; derive status_id from the FAILED/BEGIN markers and reason=InvalidLogin in the raw log.
Include a metadata object with at least metadata.version (OCSF schema version) and metadata.product.name ('VMware vCenter') in every output event.

When parsing structured key=value pairs embedded in log messages (e.g., 'VM: WebServer-Prod-042 -- user: svc-automation@vsphere.local -- result: success'), ensure regex patterns handle both 'key=value' and 'key: value' delimiters so no source values are silently dropped.

OCSF class_uid, category_uid, and type_uid must be assigned per event type/class, not hardcoded globally — build a lookup or conditional logic mapping each com.vmware.vc.* event class to the correct OCSF class.

OCSF mandates nested object structures (actor.user.name, src_endpoint.ip, dst_endpoint.hostname, metadata.product.*) — flat field extraction must be followed by object construction steps in the pipeline before output.

Every OCSF event requires a populated metadata object with at minimum product.name, product.vendor_name, and version — derive these from the known source (vcenter_host, sourcetype) during transformation.

When parsing multi-pattern log sources, ensure ALL patterns capture ALL fields — event 2's structured header fields (host, hostIP, msg, opID) were silently dropped, indicating the regex/parser did not match that log format variant.

status_id must be a numeric OCSF enum (1=Success, 2=Failure) derived from the status/log_level fields present in the source, not omitted; activity_id must reflect the specific operation (deploy, power-off, clone, auth) not a universal default of 1.
cisco_asa::ocsf: For OCSF class 4001 (Network Activity), always map permit/deny to both activity_id AND status_id (1=Success for permit, 2=Failure for deny); activity_id alone is insufficient.

Cisco ASA zone/interface prefixes (e.g. 'Outside:', 'dmz:') must be extracted and placed in src_endpoint.interface_name / dst_endpoint.interface_name — they are present in virtually every ASA log line.
ASA message-ids (e.g. 302016, 106023) and access-group/rule names must be preserved — map message-id to metadata.uid and rule name to a firewall_rule or policy field.
ICMP type and code values in ASA logs should be mapped to connection_info.icmp_type and connection_info.icmp_code in OCSF.
Emit empty container objects (traffic: {}, actor: {user: {}}, dst_endpoint: {}) only when they contain at least one populated field; omit them otherwise to keep output clean.
Validate ASA severity-to-OCSF severity_id mapping: ASA severity 1→OCSF 5 (Critical), 2→5, 3→4 (High), 4→3 (Medium), 5→2 (Low), 6→1 (Informational) — do not conflate severity levels.

Always map the permit/deny outcome from ASA logs to OCSF disposition.id (1=Blocked, 2=Allowed) and action_id — this is the most critical network security field and is always present in 106xxx/302xxx messages.

ASA severity levels are inverse to OCSF: ASA 1=Emergency→OCSF 6 Fatal, ASA 2=Critical→OCSF 5 Critical, ASA 3=Error→OCSF 4 High, ASA 4=Warning→OCSF 3 Medium, ASA 5=Notification→OCSF 2 Low, ASA 6=Informational→OCSF 1 Informational — never map ASA-6 to severity_id 5.
Interface/zone labels (e.g., 'Outside:', 'Inside:', 'dmz:') should be extracted and placed in src_endpoint.zone and dst_endpoint.zone respectively, as they are almost always present in ASA logs.
OCSF activity_id for teardown/close events should be 4 (Close) not 2 (Update); use the ASA message ID (302016=Close, 302013=Open, 106023=Deny) to drive activity_id selection.
Empty container objects ({}) should be omitted from OCSF output rather than included as empty — emit actor.user, traffic, connection_info only when at least one subfield is populated.
Always map the permit/deny outcome from ASA logs to both disposition_id (numeric) and disposition (string) — this is the single most important semantic field in firewall OCSF events.
Emit 'action' as a top-level string alongside activity_id; OCSF requires both the enum id and the human-readable string for most classification fields (severity, action, disposition).

Extract and preserve ASA-specific context fields (connection_id→connection_info.uid, access-group→firewall_rule.name, interface zone→src/dst_endpoint.zone, ICMP type/code, duration) as these are present in the raw source and meaningful in OCSF.
Omit empty stub objects ({}) rather than emitting them — OCSF treats absent fields and empty objects differently; stubs pollute the schema without adding value.
Validate ASA numeric severity (1-7, lower=more severe) to OCSF severity_id (1-6, higher=more severe) inversion carefully; ASA-4 maps to OCSF severity_id 3 (Medium/Warning), not 5 (Critical).

Always parse the syslog timestamp from the raw header (Month Day HH:MM:SS) and emit both the OCSF-mandatory integer 'time' field (epoch ms) and a correct '_time' float; never let all events share a single processing-time value.

Build a severity mapping table for the source: ASA severity 1→OCSF 6(Fatal), 2→5(Critical), 3→4(High), 4→3(Medium), 5→4(High), 6→1(Informational), 7→1(Informational) — never pass numeric levels through verbatim between schemas with different scales.

When a regex fails to match, do not emit empty endpoint/connection objects and never leak the __regex or intermediate extraction fields into the final output; add a fallback branch that at minimum preserves raw_data.

Map all structured values present in the raw log: connection ID → connection_info.uid, inbound/outbound keyword → connection_info.direction_id, duration → traffic.duration, total bytes (teardown) → traffic.bytes (not bytes_out), access-group → firewall_rule.name, syslog hostname → device.hostname, icmp type/code → connection_info.icmp_type/icmp_code.
Omit empty OCSF objects (actor.user:{}, device:{}) rather than emitting them; strict OCSF validators may reject objects that have required sub-fields if the object is present.

Always parse the syslog header timestamp (MMM DD HH:MM:SS) and convert to OCSF 'time' (epoch ms integer); never let _time default to pipeline-processing time, and never use '_time' as a substitute for the OCSF 'time' field.
Map the syslog hostname token to device.hostname in every event — it is present in every Cisco ASA message and is a required enrichment for OCSF.

Build per-message-ID extraction branches: 713019 (VPN) needs actor.user.name, session bytes, duration, and reason; 302013/302014 need connection_info.uid and direction_id; 106023/106100 need action='Denied' and policy/rule name — a single generic regex will silently drop fields for non-matching message types.
Cisco ASA severity levels map to OCSF severity_id as: ASA-1→5(Critical), ASA-2→4(High), ASA-3→3(Medium), ASA-4→3(Medium), ASA-5→2(Low), ASA-6→1(Informational) — do not treat ASA-6 as OCSF High.
Never emit empty container objects (actor:{user:{}}, device:{}, traffic:{}) — omit them or populate them; empty stubs add noise and mask extraction failures during QA.
windows_powershell::ocsf: Windows PowerShell Operational (EventCode 4103/4104) events must be mapped to OCSF Process Activity (class_uid 4007) or Script Activity, never Network Activity (4001); the presence of ComputerName/hostname does NOT indicate network traffic.
Always derive severity_id from the source EventType/Type field: Type=Information → severity_id=1 (Informational); do not default to 5 (Critical).
For PowerShell pipeline events, the 'process' OCSF object must be populated with Command Name, Script Name, and parameter bindings extracted via regex from the Message field.
Empty structural objects (src_endpoint:{}, connection_info:{}, traffic:{}) belonging to the wrong OCSF class should never be emitted; they pollute the schema and signal a class mismatch.
EventCode, RecordNumber, and SID fields must always be mapped — EventCode → metadata.event_code, SID → actor.user.uid, RecordNumber → metadata.uid or equivalent.

Windows PowerShell EventCode 4103 events must be classified as OCSF Process Activity (class_uid ~4007) or Script Activity, never Network Activity (4001); always derive category_uid and type_uid from the corrected class_uid.
Severity mapping must use the source's explicit severity/type field: EventType=4/Type=Information maps to OCSF severity_id 1 (Informational), not 5 (Critical).

All structured subfields in the Message block (User, Folder, Type, Size, Items) and context fields (Command Name, Script Name, Host Application, Runspace ID, Pipeline ID, Sequence Number, Engine Version, SID) must be parsed and mapped to OCSF process/actor/metadata fields rather than dropped.
Never populate ip-typed OCSF fields with hostnames; use endpoint.hostname for hostnames and endpoint.ip only for valid IP addresses.
Empty network-specific container fields (src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, connection_info, traffic) must be omitted entirely when the source event is not a network event.

For Windows PowerShell Operational logs (EventCode 4103/4104), use OCSF class_uid 4007 (Process Activity) or 3006 (Script Activity), never 4001 (Network Activity) — class selection must be driven by the log source type, not a generic default.
Severity mapping must consume the source's Type/Severity fields: EventType=4/Type=Information/Severity=Informational must map to OCSF severity_id 1 (Informational), not 5 (Critical).

The Message field in PowerShell logs is the primary data carrier and must be parsed: CommandInvocation, ParameterBinding, Script Name, Command Name, Host Application, Engine Version, Pipeline ID, Sequence Number, and Runspace ID should all be extracted to appropriate OCSF fields (process.*, file.path, metadata.*, etc.).
Never populate a hostname string into an IP-typed field (dst_endpoint.ip); hostname belongs in dst_endpoint.hostname, and for a local script execution event, even dst_endpoint is semantically wrong.
User SID fields (Sid=) must always be mapped to actor.user.uid in OCSF; domain-qualified usernames (AD\SYSTEM) must split domain into actor.user.domain and name into actor.user.name.
cisco_esa::ocsf: Cisco ESA events must map to OCSF Email Activity class (class_uid 9007, category_uid 9) not Network Activity (4001/4); always verify class selection against the event's domain before building field mappings.

Severity parsing must be a mandatory first step for any syslog-style source: extract the syslog severity keyword (Info, Critical, Warning, etc.) and map it to OCSF severity_id before any other field; a null severity_id on a Critical event is a critical gap.

Every extractable field from the raw line (MID, ICID, Subject, spam score, verdict, bytes) must have an explicit mapping rule; do not emit empty objects ({}) for structured sub-fields — either populate them or omit them to avoid false schema compliance signals.

Email-specific metadata (subject, message ID, spam/AV verdicts, quarantine actions) belongs in an 'email' object or 'findings' array in OCSF; mapping sender only to actor.user loses the email semantics and leaves the bulk of ESA-specific telemetry unmapped.

For Cisco ESA logs targeting OCSF class 4001, always parse and map MID→email.message_uid, ICID→src_endpoint connection identifier, DCID→dst_endpoint connection identifier, and SMTP response codes→email status fields before emitting the event.

Never emit null for severity_id in OCSF; map log-level keywords (Info, Warning, Critical) to the corresponding OCSF severity_id integer (1=Informational, 2=Low, 3=Medium, 4=High, 5=Critical, 6=Fatal) as a fallback.
Verify activity_id enum values against the specific OCSF class definition — for Email Activity (4001), 'message done/delivered' should map to Deliver (2), not Send (1).

Remove or populate empty nested objects (src_endpoint, dst_endpoint, connection_info, traffic, actor.user) — empty objects in OCSF output indicate the pipeline skeleton was built but the extraction regexes were never wired up.
Preserve the original _raw field in OCSF output under unmapped or raw_data to enable auditability and reprocessing.
Always parse and map all named fields in the log line (DCID, MID, RID, IP, port) before emitting OCSF output — empty container objects score as failures.
Map the syslog severity keyword ('Info', 'Warning', 'Critical') to the OCSF severity_id integer; null is never acceptable when the source explicitly provides a level.
For Cisco ESA email logs, prefer OCSF class_uid 4009 (Email Activity) over generic network activity classes; class selection should be driven by source log semantics.
Preserve the raw message text in the OCSF 'message' field so no source information is silently discarded.
Omit or null empty container objects (src_endpoint: {}, traffic: {}, actor.user: {}) rather than emitting them empty — they mislead consumers into thinking data was evaluated and found absent.
windows_security::ocsf: Route each Windows Security EventID to its correct OCSF class_uid before setting activity_id and type_uid: 4624/4634/4648/4776 → class 3002 (Authentication Activity); 4672 → class 3003 (Authorize Session); type_uid = class_uid * 100 + activity_id.
Never place a hostname string in an 'ip' field; use dst_endpoint.hostname for Computer/WorkstationName and only populate dst_endpoint.ip when an actual IP address is available.

Map ALL parsed XML fields from EventData: UserSid→user.uid, DomainName→user.domain, LogonType→logon_type_id, LogonId→session.uid, ProcessName/ProcessId→process object, AuthenticationPackageName→auth_protocol, PrivilegeList→privileges, Status→status/status_id.
Windows Security Audit events (Level=0) are Informational; set severity_id=1 by default, not 5 (Critical).
Always emit metadata.event_code with the original EventID and a top-level OCSF 'time' (integer epoch ms) field distinct from Cribl's internal '_time'.

Branch pipeline logic by EventID (4624=Authentication Logon, 4634=Authentication Logoff, 4672=Privilege Assignment, 4776=Credential Validation, 4648=Explicit Credential Logon) and set class_uid, activity_id, type_uid, and severity_id accordingly per event type.

For authentication events, maintain the distinction between SubjectUser* (actor/initiator → actor.user.*) and TargetUser* (authenticated account → user.*); never collapse them into a single actor.user.name.
Never place a hostname in an .ip field; map Computer/hostname values to *.hostname fields and only real IP addresses to *.ip fields. Always populate metadata.event_code with the EventID value.

Empty structural objects (connection_info:{}, traffic:{}) should either be omitted or populated; leaving them empty while source fields like WorkstationName and LogonProcessName exist is a mapping gap.

Windows Security events map to multiple OCSF classes: 4624/4625/4634/4768 → Authentication (3002), 4688 → Process Activity (1007), 4672 → Authorize Session (3003), 4720/4722/4725 → Account Change (3001); a single class_uid for all event IDs is always wrong.

type_uid must always equal class_uid * 100 + activity_id, and activity_id must reflect the semantic outcome (logon success=1, logon fail=2, logoff=4, create=1 within its class, etc.) not default to 1.
Separate the OCSF actor (SubjectUserName — the initiator) from the target user (TargetUserName — the object of the action); conflating them corrupts who-did-what-to-whom semantics.
dst_endpoint.ip must contain an IP address; hostnames belong in dst_endpoint.hostname (or device.hostname); never store a FQDN string in an IP field.

Event-class-specific fields (CommandLine, NewProcessName, TicketOptions, PrivilegeList, FailureReason, LogonType, Status) must be extracted per EventID in dedicated pipeline branches, not ignored; they constitute the primary forensic value of each event.
Always emit the original event ID in metadata.event_code and map Status hex codes to OCSF status/status_id to preserve success/failure semantics.
linux_audit::ocsf: Always validate that the declared sourcetype matches the actual log format before applying a pipeline — a linux_audit pipeline must not process CyberArk IDP JSON events.
Timestamp must be derived from the source event's time field (here: `timestamp` in milliseconds → divide by 1000 for Unix seconds); never use processing/ingest time as _time.

All key identity fields (username, userId/email, source IP, uuid, action, message) must be explicitly mapped to OCSF target fields (actor.user.name, actor.user.email_addr, src_endpoint.ip, metadata.uid, activity_name, message) — they will not auto-populate.

OCSF class_uid must reflect actual event semantics: identity/provisioning events belong in Account Change (3005) or similar, not Network Activity (4001); metadata.product should reflect the actual originating application.

Empty object stubs (src_endpoint:{}, traffic:{}, connection_info:{}) should only be included when the source actually provides values for those objects, or they should be omitted to avoid misleading consumers.

Parse the `type=` field first and branch classification: SYSCALL/EXECVE → class_uid 4007 (Process Activity), USER_AUTH → 3002 (Authentication), PATH/CWD → 1001 (File System Activity); never apply a single static class_uid to all linux_audit record types.

Linux audit records encode user context in uid/auid/euid fields — these must be mapped to actor.user.uid, actor.user.uid_alt, and actor.user.name; process context (pid, ppid, exe, comm) must populate a process object; never leave these as empty objects.
Always map outcome/result fields: success=yes/no maps to status_id 1/2, res=failed maps to status_id 2 — omitting status_id means security-critical failure context is silently lost.
For USER_AUTH records, extract the embedded inner fields (acct, hostname, addr, exe, op) from the msg='' quoted string using a secondary regex parse pass, not just the outer key=value pairs.

Empty container objects (src_endpoint={}, connection_info={}, traffic={}) should be omitted from output events where the source record type carries no such data, to avoid misleading consumers of the OCSF output.
nginx_access::ocsf: Always parse the raw nginx log line with a regex or grok before mapping to OCSF; without parsing, all structured fields remain empty even if the OCSF skeleton is correct.
The OCSF 'time' field is mandatory and must be an integer epoch-milliseconds value derived from the log timestamp, not left null — ensure the timestamp parser runs before the OCSF mapping step.

Map src_endpoint.ip from the client IP, dst_endpoint.hostname from the virtual host, http_request.{http_method,url,version} from the request line, and http_response.code + traffic.bytes_out from status/bytes fields — these are the minimum viable fields for an HTTP Activity event.
Do not hardcode severity_id; derive it dynamically from the HTTP status code (e.g., 4xx → informational or medium, 5xx → high) to preserve the signal present in the source.
metadata.product.name should reflect the actual software product ('nginx'), not a category label like 'Security'; vendor_name should be 'F5/NGINX' or 'nginx'.
Always validate that the regex or parser step actually extracts named fields before writing mapping logic; empty objects in output nearly always indicate the parse step silently failed.

The OCSF 'time' field must be derived from the log timestamp (parsed and converted to epoch ms), never left null; use strptime or equivalent on the bracketed timestamp field immediately after extraction.

For nginx combined+upstream format, a single regex must capture all positional fields: client_ip, ident, auth_user, time_local, method, uri, protocol, status, bytes_sent, http_referer, http_user_agent, upstream_addr, request_time, upstream_response_time, vhost — map each to its OCSF counterpart explicitly.
HTTP method should drive activity_id: GET→1(Open/Read), POST→2(Create), DELETE→4(Delete), CONNECT→99(Other) — never hardcode a single value.
_time must be set from the parsed log timestamp, not the pipeline processing time, to ensure correct chronological ordering and deduplication.
citrix_netscaler::cim: Always parse and set _time as a valid epoch timestamp from the raw timestamp field — a null _time makes all CIM events functionally unusable regardless of how well other fields are mapped.
Map action by inspecting the full event sub-type token (e.g., SSL_HANDSHAKE_SUCCESS → 'allowed'/'success', SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE → 'blocked'/'failure') rather than defaulting all to 'failure'.
Preserve the full original event sub-type string in event_type and vendor_action (e.g., 'SSL_HANDSHAKE_SUCCESS', not 'SSL_HANDSHAKE') to avoid losing source-level specificity.

For backend NetScaler SSL events, detect the 'Backend' keyword and swap the field mappings: ServerIP → dest/dst_ip, ServerPort → dest_port/dst_port, and map certificate fields (SerialNumber, ValidFrom, ValidTo, SignatureAlgorithm) to their CIM equivalents.

CIM 'app' should reflect the application protocol (e.g., 'ssl'), not the log subsystem name ('SSLLOG'); use transport/protocol fields appropriately and avoid inventing non-CIM structural fields like 'object' or 'class_uid' with string labels.

Trim whitespace from extracted values (e.g., certificate SubjectName/IssuerName) and normalize units — HandshakeTime in ms should be divided by 1000 or stored in a separate ms field, not silently aliased to CIM 'duration' which implies seconds.
Always parse and populate _time from the syslog timestamp as epoch; a null _time makes events unsearchable in Splunk CIM — test timestamp parsing as the first pipeline validation step.
Map action from the full event subtype token (SSL_HANDSHAKE_SUCCESS → 'allowed/success', SSL_HANDSHAKE_FAILURE → 'blocked/failure'); never default to 'failure' when the raw token contains SUCCESS.

Preserve the full event subtype string (SSL_HANDSHAKE_SUCCESS, SSL_HANDSHAKE_SUBJECTNAME) in vendor_action and derive event_type/signature from it; truncating the suffix loses semantically critical distinctions.

Do not mix OCSF schema fields (class_uid with numeric values) into a Splunk CIM output — choose one target schema and use only its canonical field names; string values for class_uid are invalid in OCSF.
CIM 'signature' = event signature/ID (the event type string), not the cipher suite; map cipher suite to a dedicated field like ssl_cipher and signature to the event type identifier.

For backend SSL events, always extract and map certificate fields (SerialNumber→cert_serial, ValidFrom→cert_valid_from, ValidTo→cert_valid_to, SignatureAlgorithm→ssl_sign_alg) — these are high-value security fields present in the source.
f5_bigip::ocsf: OCSF Network Activity (4001) mandates nested objects: src_endpoint{ip,port}, dst_endpoint{ip,port}, metadata{version,product}, and optionally connection_info{protocol_id} — flat IP/port fields are non-compliant.

When parsing syslog timestamps without an explicit year, default to the most recent plausible calendar year (e.g., current year) rather than allowing the epoch to land in 2001; validate _time output is within a reasonable range.

Not all F5 BIG-IP syslog lines are Network Activity — httpd access logs should map to Web Resources Activity (6001) or HTTP Activity, syslog-ng/mcpd config events to System Activity (1001); use msg_id prefix and process name to discriminate class_uid.

The OCSF 'metadata' object is mandatory for all events and must include at minimum 'version' (e.g., '1.0.0') and 'product.name'; its absence makes every output event schema-invalid regardless of other field accuracy.

Syslog severity keywords (info/notice/warning/err/crit) must be mapped to OCSF severity_id (0-6) consistently: info→1, notice→2, warning→3, error→4, critical→5, fatal→6; do not conflate with the BIG-IP message-ID numeric suffix which is a different scale.
alibaba_cloud_actiontrail::xsiam: Every XSIAM passthrough pipeline for a cataloged source MUST explicitly set __sourceIdentifier, __vendor, and __product as static literal fields — these are not inferred automatically by Cribl and will not appear unless a Eval/Set function assigns them.

Timestamp (_time) must be parsed from the source event's own time field (eventTime in this case) using strptime or equivalent; never rely on Cribl's default wall-clock assignment for audit/trail logs where event time accuracy is critical.
Always validate _raw completeness for every output event; truncated JSON in _raw will cause XSIAM ingestion parsing failures and data loss for the affected events.
When using Cribl Pipeline Preview to validate, confirm all three routing tags are present before promotion — their absence is silent at pipeline level but fatal at XSIAM ingest routing.

Never mutate or replace _raw — it must be set to the original, unmodified vendor event string (or serialized JSON blob) before any other processing step; a Eval/Serialize step should assign _raw = JSON.stringify(event) from the raw input, not from a partially transformed object.

Always parse the vendor timestamp field (eventTime for Alibaba ActionTrail) and assign it to _time using a timestamp parser or Eval; leaving _time as null causes events to be dropped or misindexed in XSIAM.

When wrapping source fields under a nested key (e.g. 'event'), ensure all required catalog JSON paths (event.eventId, event.eventType, event.eventName) are actually populated with source values before the event exits the pipeline.
Validate pipeline output in preview against at least one real sample event to catch cases where transformation logic produces empty/stub objects instead of forwarding actual field values.
